biomes.name: Open-ocean bacterioplankton
biomes.note: A sea run by cyanobacteria and small algae; no zooplankton grazers, so the water column is thin and clear.

biomes.name: Stromatolite carbonate platform
biomes.note: Microbial reefs still build the shelves, but they are past their peak and slowly losing ground to grazing and burrowing that has not arrived yet.

biomes.name: Anoxic sulphidic mid-depth ocean
biomes.note: Below a thin oxygenated skin the ocean is ferruginous to euxinic -- the 'Canfield ocean' -- and hostile to anything needing oxygen.

biomes.name: Bare regolith and desert pavement
biomes.note: Land is rock, sand and lag gravel. Rivers run in wide braided sheets with nothing to hold their banks.

biomes.name: Microbial land crust
biomes.note: Thin cyanobacterial and probably early fungal films on damp rock and floodplain silt -- the only life above the tideline.

biomes.name: Evaporite sabkha
biomes.note: Vast hypersaline flats on the margins of Rodinia, precipitating gypsum and halite under a dry supercontinental sky.

biomes.name: Open-ocean bacterioplankton
biomes.note: Acritarchs -- resting cysts of early algae -- become common enough to be a usable fossil record.

biomes.name: Stromatolite carbonate platform
biomes.note: Microbialite reefs fringe the rifting margins of Rodinia in warm shallow water.

biomes.name: Anoxic sulphidic mid-depth ocean
biomes.note: Oxygen is still confined to the surface mixed layer; the deep sea is uninhabitable by animal standards.

biomes.name: Microbial land crust
biomes.note: Crusts thicken on stable surfaces; vase-shaped microfossils show protists are now hunting each other in shallow water.

biomes.name: Bare regolith and desert pavement
biomes.note: Weathering is chemical and mechanical only -- no roots, no soil profile in the modern sense.

biomes.name: Rift-margin lagoon
biomes.note: Rodinia's tearing interior floods repeatedly, making restricted basins with their own microbial communities.

biomes.name: Open-ocean bacterioplankton
biomes.note: Eukaryotic phytoplankton diversity is rising; the ocean is warming and CO2 is thousands of ppm.

biomes.name: Stromatolite carbonate platform
biomes.note: Still the dominant reef-builder on Earth, and will be for another two hundred million years.

biomes.name: Anoxic sulphidic mid-depth ocean
biomes.note: Widespread euxinia; the redox structure of the ocean has barely changed since the Mesoproterozoic.

biomes.name: Rift-valley lake and floodplain
biomes.note: Rodinia is coming apart, and the new rift basins hold the first substantial non-marine sedimentary records.

biomes.name: Bare regolith and desert pavement
biomes.note: A hot, dry, plantless land surface veined with braided rivers.

biomes.name: Microbial land crust
biomes.note: Damp-substrate crusts, likely including early fungi and possibly the first terrestrial algae.

biomes.name: Open-ocean bacterioplankton
biomes.note: The last normal ocean before the freeze; the Franklin basalts are already erupting across tropical Laurentia.

biomes.name: Stromatolite carbonate platform
biomes.note: Carbonate factories are running at full rate right up to the glacial onset -- the transition is abrupt.

biomes.name: Expanding sea ice
biomes.note: Ice begins spreading from both poles far faster than the carbonate platforms can retreat.

biomes.name: Glacial outwash plain
biomes.note: Ice-marginal sand and gravel sheets appear on continents that have never seen a glacier this large.

biomes.name: Anoxic sulphidic mid-depth ocean
biomes.note: Deep water is still anoxic, and about to be sealed under a lid of ice.

biomes.name: Bare regolith and desert pavement
biomes.note: Fresh basalt weathering in the tropics is drawing CO2 down hard -- the land surface is the murder weapon.

biomes.name: Global sea ice
biomes.note: The Sturtian at its deepest: ice reaches the equator, and the ocean surface is frozen or near-frozen worldwide.

biomes.name: Sub-ice ocean
biomes.note: A dark, cold, oxygen-poor sea under a kilometre of ice, cut off from the atmosphere for millions of years.

biomes.name: Cryoconite and supraglacial meltpond
biomes.note: Dust-darkened pits on the ice surface -- meltwater refugia where photosynthesis can still run.

biomes.name: Ice-free tropical refugium
biomes.note: Narrow open-water or thin-ice bands near the equator, the leading explanation for how photosynthetic life survived at all.

biomes.name: Subglacial and grounding-line seafloor
biomes.note: Iron formations return after a billion-year absence, because anoxic iron-rich water has nowhere to oxidise.

biomes.name: Ice-scoured bedrock
biomes.note: Land is stripped rock under a continental ice sheet; no crust, no weathering, no CO2 drawdown -- which is how the freeze eventually ends.

biomes.name: Open shelf sea
biomes.note: The non-glacial interlude between the two snowballs is real: normal marine sedimentation resumes for several million years.

biomes.name: Post-glacial cap carbonate platform
biomes.note: Enormous carbonate precipitation as a super-greenhouse atmosphere is titrated by a suddenly deglaciated world.

biomes.name: Meltwater-stratified surface ocean
biomes.note: A fresh, buoyant lid over dense saline deep water, poorly mixed and chemically strange.

biomes.name: Glacial outwash plain
biomes.note: Freshly deglaciated continents shedding vast volumes of poorly-sorted debris.

biomes.name: Microbial land crust
biomes.note: Crusts recolonise scoured rock surfaces wherever meltwater keeps them damp.

biomes.name: Anoxic sulphidic basin
biomes.note: Deep water is still anoxic and now loaded with iron and sulphide flushed off the land.

biomes.name: Expanding sea ice
biomes.note: The Marinoan begins; ice advances again toward the tropics after the interlude.

biomes.name: Global sea ice
biomes.note: Within a few million years the ocean surface is once more largely frozen.

biomes.name: Sub-ice ocean
biomes.note: A second long isolation of the marine biosphere beneath ice.

biomes.name: Cryoconite and supraglacial meltpond
biomes.note: Again the best-argued refuge for eukaryotic algae through the freeze.

biomes.name: Ice-scoured bedrock
biomes.note: Continents under ice, weathering shut down, CO2 accumulating toward the escape threshold.

biomes.name: Subglacial seafloor
biomes.note: Glaciomarine diamictites, dropstones and iron-rich sediment worldwide.

biomes.name: Post-glacial cap carbonate platform
biomes.note: The Marinoan ends catastrophically fast; cap dolostones blanket tillites on every continent.

biomes.name: Super-greenhouse tropical ocean
biomes.note: Tens of thousands of ppm CO2 and a surface ocean that goes from freezing to sweltering in geological instants.

biomes.name: Meltwater-stratified surface ocean
biomes.note: Ice sheets collapse and dump freshwater faster than the ocean can mix it.

biomes.name: Glacial outwash plain
biomes.note: Continents draining an entire planet's worth of melting ice.

biomes.name: Microbial land crust
biomes.note: The land surface begins to be recolonised; oxygen is starting its Neoproterozoic rise.

biomes.name: Oxygenating shelf sea
biomes.note: Oxygen levels climb into a range that will, for the first time, permit large motile animals.

biomes.name: Oxygenating shelf sea
biomes.note: Deep oxygenation is patchy and pulsed, but the shelves now hold enough oxygen for centimetre-scale eukaryotes.

biomes.name: Microbial mat seafloor
biomes.note: Undisturbed 'elephant-skin' mats carpet the seabed -- nothing burrows yet, so the sediment-water interface is a hard, sealed surface.

biomes.name: Phosphogenic shelf
biomes.note: The Doushantuo phosphorites preserve embryos, acritarchs and multicellular algae in cellular detail.

biomes.name: Stromatolite carbonate platform
biomes.note: Still a major reef system, but multicellular life is now competing for the same sunlit real estate.

biomes.name: Anoxic black-shale basin
biomes.note: Below the oxygenated shelf, euxinic basins persist and expand and contract on short timescales.

biomes.name: Bare regolith and microbial crust
biomes.note: Land is unchanged from a billion years earlier: crusted rock, braided rivers, no vegetation.

biomes.name: Microbial mat seafloor
biomes.note: The Ediacaran seafloor is a mat-bound world -- most Ediacaran organisms lie on it, graze it, or root into it.

biomes.name: Ediacaran deep-shelf garden
biomes.note: Below the photic zone at Mistaken Point, fractal rangeomorphs stand in dense stands feeding on dissolved organics.

biomes.name: Shallow Ediacaran shelf
biomes.note: The White Sea assemblage: Dickinsonia, Kimberella and the first convincing tracks of an animal moving under its own power.

biomes.name: Stromatolite carbonate platform
biomes.note: Microbial reefs persist, and at the very end of the Ediacaran get their first skeletal competitor in Cloudina.

biomes.name: Anoxic black-shale basin
biomes.note: Oxygen minimum zones remain broad; the ocean is oxygenated in the shallows and hostile below.

biomes.name: Bare regolith and desert pavement
biomes.note: Land remains lifeless above the crust level, and rivers still cannot hold a channel.

biomes.name: Open shelf sea
biomes.note: The Cambrian explosion is under way: the shelves fill with mobile, armoured, predatory animals within a few million years.

biomes.name: Bioturbated seafloor
biomes.note: The 'agronomic revolution' -- burrowing shreds the mat world, ending three billion years of sealed seabed.

biomes.name: Archaeocyath reef
biomes.note: The first animal-built reef framework, made by sponge-grade calcareous archaeocyaths on tropical Siberia and Laurentia.

biomes.name: Epeiric carbonate platform
biomes.note: Sea level is rising hard; shallow seas flood continental interiors and become the main habitat on Earth.

biomes.name: Anoxic black-shale basin
biomes.note: Repeated anoxic pulses onto the shelf drive several early Cambrian extinction events.

biomes.name: Bare regolith and desert pavement
biomes.note: Land is still rock. Everything interesting is happening under water.

biomes.name: Open shelf sea
biomes.note: Trilobite-dominated shelf faunas worldwide; the Chengjiang and Burgess-type communities are the full ecosystem, not a curiosity.

biomes.name: Bioturbated seafloor
biomes.note: Burrowing deepens, oxygenating sediment and permanently changing marine chemistry.

biomes.name: Archaeocyath reef
biomes.note: Archaeocyath framework reefs collapse near the end of the Early Cambrian and are not replaced for millions of years.

biomes.name: Epeiric carbonate platform
biomes.note: The Sauk transgression drowns Laurentia under clean, warm, sediment-starved carbonate seas.

biomes.name: Nektonic water column
biomes.note: Anomalocaridids and the first swimming predators open the water column as a habitat for the first time.

biomes.name: Desert pavement and ephemeral wadi
biomes.note: Land: bare, hot, wind-scoured, with sheetflood deposits and nothing to slow the water.

biomes.name: Epeiric carbonate platform
biomes.note: Vast, shallow, warm and low-relief -- the defining marine habitat of the Early Palaeozoic.

biomes.name: Open shelf sea
biomes.note: The post-Cambrian lull before the Ordovician radiation; conodonts and brachiopods are quietly diversifying.

biomes.name: Microbial-sponge reef
biomes.note: With archaeocyaths gone, reefs revert to stromatolites, calcimicrobes and lithistid sponges.

biomes.name: Anoxic black-shale basin
biomes.note: Deep basins stay anoxic; graptolite shales begin accumulating in the slope settings.

biomes.name: Planktic water column
biomes.note: Graptolites take up permanent residence in open water, and become the finest biostratigraphic clock of the era.

biomes.name: Bare regolith and desert pavement
biomes.note: Still no land vegetation, though spore evidence for the first liverwort-grade plants is only twenty million years away.

biomes.name: Epeiric carbonate platform
biomes.note: The Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event at full tilt: bryozoans, crinoids, brachiopods and corals stack the shelf into tiered communities.

biomes.name: Bryozoan-crinoid meadow
biomes.note: Dense, waist-high sessile filter-feeder gardens -- the Palaeozoic equivalent of a seagrass bed, made entirely of animals.

biomes.name: Stromatoporoid-coral reef
biomes.note: Rugose and tabulate corals join stromatoporoid sponges to build the first reefs that would look familiar to a diver.

biomes.name: Anoxic black-shale basin
biomes.note: Graptolitic black shales spread widely across drowned continental margins.

biomes.name: Cryptogamic ground cover
biomes.note: The first true land plants -- non-vascular, liverwort-grade, millimetres tall -- appear as spore assemblages in Ordovician rocks.

biomes.name: Bare regolith and desert pavement
biomes.note: Ground cover is patchy and confined to damp margins; most of the land surface is still stone.

biomes.name: Continental ice sheet
biomes.note: The Hirnantian glaciation drops an ice cap over Saharan Gondwana and pulls sea level down a hundred metres.

biomes.name: Sea ice
biomes.note: Ice extends well into mid-latitudes; the epeiric seas that held most marine life simply drain away.

biomes.name: Cold-water Hirnantia shelf
biomes.note: A low-diversity, cosmopolitan cold-water brachiopod fauna replaces the rich tropical communities.

biomes.name: Anoxic black-shale basin
biomes.note: The second extinction pulse comes from anoxia flooding the shelves as the ice melts back.

biomes.name: Exposed carbonate platform
biomes.note: Drowned platforms are exposed, karstified, and their ecosystems destroyed -- the first great mass extinction.

biomes.name: Cryptogamic ground cover
biomes.note: Early land plants survive the crisis; some argue their weathering caused it.

biomes.name: Epeiric carbonate platform
biomes.note: Sea level rebounds; warm shallow seas return across Laurentia, Baltica and Siberia.

biomes.name: Stromatoporoid-coral reef
biomes.note: The Silurian is a reef golden age -- Gotland and the Michigan Basin pinnacle reefs are built now.

biomes.name: Cryptogamic ground cover and rhyniophyte patch
biomes.note: Cooksonia and its relatives: leafless, rootless, centimetre-high vascular stems clustered in damp low ground.

biomes.name: Eurypterid lagoon
biomes.note: Restricted, brackish, hypersaline basins where sea scorpions up to two metres long dominate.

biomes.name: Anoxic black-shale basin
biomes.note: Recurrent oceanic anoxic events punctuate the Silurian and drive graptolite extinctions.

biomes.name: Bare regolith and desert pavement
biomes.note: Vegetation is still confined to a green fuzz along water; the interior is barren.

biomes.name: Rhyniophyte marsh
biomes.note: Low, dense, ankle-height vascular vegetation in permanently wet ground -- the first plant community with structure.

biomes.name: Hot-spring sinter wetland
biomes.note: The Rhynie chert setting: geothermal silica entombing whole plants, mites, springtails and fungi in growth position.

biomes.name: Epeiric carbonate platform
biomes.note: Shallow tropical seas remain the largest habitat on the planet.

biomes.name: Stromatoporoid-coral reef
biomes.note: Reef systems are at their greatest Palaeozoic extent -- larger in area than the modern reef belt.

biomes.name: Old Red Sandstone floodplain
biomes.note: Braided rivers on a red, seasonally arid alluvial plain, now with just enough plant cover to begin holding banks.

biomes.name: Freshwater fish habitat
biomes.note: Rivers and lakes fill with placoderms, acanthodians and early lobe-fins -- the Devonian is the Age of Fishes.

biomes.name: Zosterophyll and trimerophyte marsh
biomes.note: Vegetation is knee-high, branching and spreading laterally by rhizome; still no leaves worth the name.

biomes.name: Epeiric carbonate platform
biomes.note: Warm, wide and productive, ringed by the largest reef tracts of the Palaeozoic.

biomes.name: Stromatoporoid-coral reef
biomes.note: Devonian reefs like the Canning Basin build kilometre-scale complexes with fore-reef slopes and back-reef lagoons.

biomes.name: Old Red Sandstone floodplain
biomes.note: Meandering channels appear for the first time in Earth history, because plants finally make cohesive banks.

biomes.name: Freshwater lake and river
biomes.note: Diverse fish faunas; the fin-to-limb transition is under way in shallow vegetated water.

biomes.name: Desert pavement and erg
biomes.note: Continental interiors remain arid and largely plantless.

biomes.name: Archaeopteris forest
biomes.note: The first forest: trees eight metres tall with real wood, real roots and a leaf canopy, casting the first shade on Earth.

biomes.name: Cladoxylopsid stand
biomes.note: Wattieza-type trees at Gilboa -- palm-like trunks with frond crowns, forming the earliest known tree stands.

biomes.name: Progymnosperm floodplain woodland
biomes.note: Rooting depth increases sharply, weathering rates jump, and soil profiles become recognisable.

biomes.name: Stromatoporoid-coral reef
biomes.note: Reefs are still enormous, but nutrient runoff from the newly forested land is starting to eutrophy the shelves.

biomes.name: Epeiric carbonate platform
biomes.note: Widespread and warm, with high sea level flooding continental interiors.

biomes.name: Anoxic black-shale basin
biomes.note: Black shales expand across shelves as land-derived nutrients drive plankton blooms and bottom-water anoxia.

biomes.name: Anoxic black-shale basin
biomes.note: The Frasnian-Famennian crisis: repeated anoxic events across the world's shelves, recorded in the Kellwasser black shales.

biomes.name: Collapsing reef system
biomes.note: Stromatoporoid-coral reefs are destroyed and will not be rebuilt at this scale for a hundred million years.

biomes.name: Archaeopteris forest
biomes.note: Forests are now widespread and are the leading suspect in the reef collapse, via runoff and CO2 drawdown.

biomes.name: Progymnosperm floodplain woodland
biomes.note: Root systems reach a metre or more, restructuring the entire land surface.

biomes.name: Freshwater swamp
biomes.note: The habitat where the first tetrapods live -- shallow, vegetated, oxygen-poor water where air-breathing pays.

biomes.name: Epeiric shelf sea
biomes.note: Marine communities are impoverished; the Late Devonian is a long extinction, not a single event.

biomes.name: Archaeopteris forest and early seed-plant woodland
biomes.note: Seed plants have arrived, freeing reproduction from standing water and opening drier ground.

biomes.name: Freshwater swamp
biomes.note: Romer's Gap: tetrapods are here but barely fossilised, in coal-poor, oxygen-poor wetlands.

biomes.name: Epeiric shelf sea
biomes.note: The Hangenberg event closes the Devonian, wiping out placoderms entirely.

biomes.name: Anoxic black-shale basin
biomes.note: One more anoxic pulse at the Devonian-Carboniferous boundary.

biomes.name: Glaciated highland
biomes.note: Ice begins forming on high-latitude Gondwana -- the opening of the Late Palaeozoic Ice Age.

biomes.name: Coastal peat mire
biomes.note: The first substantial peat accumulation; the coal-forming machinery of the Carboniferous is starting up.

biomes.name: Lycopsid coal swamp
biomes.note: Waterlogged tropical mires where Lepidodendron grows thirty metres in a few years and falls over; peat accumulates faster than it can rot.

biomes.name: Epeiric carbonate platform
biomes.note: The Mississippian is the great crinoid limestone interval -- shelf seas floored by metres of shattered crinoid stems.

biomes.name: Crinoid meadow
biomes.note: Echinoderm gardens so dense their debris becomes the rock itself.

biomes.name: Continental ice sheet
biomes.note: Gondwanan ice grows toward its Late Palaeozoic maximum; sea level swings become the dominant control on shelf sedimentation.

biomes.name: Seed-fern floodplain woodland
biomes.note: Drier ground away from the mires supports pteridosperms and early conifer relatives.

biomes.name: Anoxic black-shale basin
biomes.note: Cyclic flooding lays down widespread organic-rich shales between the coals.

biomes.name: Lycopsid coal swamp
biomes.note: The single most productive terrestrial biome in Earth's history; nearly all the world's coal is being made right now.

biomes.name: Tropical everwet rainforest
biomes.note: Multi-tiered forest of lycopsids, tree ferns, calamiteans and seed ferns straddling the wet equatorial belt.

biomes.name: Continental ice sheet
biomes.note: The Late Palaeozoic Ice Age at full strength over southern Gondwana; glacial-interglacial cycles drive the coal cyclothems.

biomes.name: Epeiric carbonate platform
biomes.note: Repeatedly flooded and drained on a hundred-thousand-year beat as the ice waxes and wanes.

biomes.name: High-oxygen fire-prone woodland
biomes.note: Oxygen above thirty percent means charcoal in almost every coal seam, and insects that can grow to absurd size.

biomes.name: Cold-temperate Gondwanan tundra
biomes.note: Beyond the ice margin, a sparse cold flora on periglacial ground -- nothing like the tropical swamps.

biomes.name: Lycopsid coal swamp
biomes.note: Peak coal, and near its end: the Carboniferous Rainforest Collapse fragments this biome within a few million years.

biomes.name: Tropical everwet rainforest
biomes.note: Rainforest breaks into isolated refugia as the climate dries; tree ferns replace lycopsids, and tetrapod faunas diverge in isolation.

biomes.name: Seed-fern and conifer dry woodland
biomes.note: Drought-tolerant seed plants expand onto ground the swamp flora cannot hold.

biomes.name: Continental ice sheet
biomes.note: Gondwanan ice near maximum extent, with a possible smaller northern-hemisphere counterpart.

biomes.name: Epeiric carbonate platform
biomes.note: Cyclothemic shelf seas across Pangaea's tropical interior.

biomes.name: Cold-temperate Gondwanan flora
biomes.note: The first Glossopteris-grade vegetation colonising deglaciated ground in the high south.

biomes.name: Glossopteris cold-temperate forest
biomes.note: Deciduous seed-fern woodland spreading across deglaciating Gondwana -- a genuinely seasonal, high-latitude forest biome.

biomes.name: Desert erg and playa
biomes.note: Pangaea's interior is now vast, continental and hyperarid; dune fields the size of countries.

biomes.name: Seed-fern and conifer dry woodland
biomes.note: Voltzialean conifers take the drier uplands; the everwet flora is a shrinking tropical relic.

biomes.name: Continental ice sheet
biomes.note: Gondwanan ice is in retreat, surviving mainly over Australia and Antarctica.

biomes.name: Epeiric carbonate platform
biomes.note: Warm shelf seas around Pangaea's margins and in the Tethyan embayment.

biomes.name: Hypersaline evaporite basin
biomes.note: Restricted arms of the sea evaporate to salt in the continental interior.

biomes.name: Desert erg and playa
biomes.note: The most arid continental interior of the Phanerozoic; the Permian red beds are laid down under it.

biomes.name: Glossopteris cold-temperate forest
biomes.note: The dominant high-southern vegetation, and the flora whose distribution first suggested Gondwana existed.

biomes.name: Cathaysian tropical everwet forest
biomes.note: An isolated wet-tropical flora on the Chinese blocks, with Gigantopteris -- the last refuge of everwet forest.

biomes.name: Conifer upland woodland
biomes.note: Walchian conifers on well-drained slopes -- the beginnings of a recognisably modern-looking forest structure.

biomes.name: Epeiric carbonate platform
biomes.note: Rich Permian shelf faunas: fusulinid foraminifera, bryozoan-sponge reefs like the Capitan.

biomes.name: Sponge-algal reef
biomes.note: The Permian reef style is bryozoan, sponge and calcareous algae, not coral -- and it disappears entirely at the end of the period.

biomes.name: Desert erg and playa
biomes.note: Arid interior at its most extensive, with the Zechstein and Kazanian evaporites forming on the margins.

biomes.name: Glossopteris cold-temperate forest
biomes.note: Still the great southern forest, and about to be annihilated along with every other peat-forming flora.

biomes.name: Cathaysian tropical everwet forest
biomes.note: Erupting Emeishan basalts begin to disrupt the South China wet tropics; the end-Guadalupian extinction hits here first.

biomes.name: Sponge-algal reef
biomes.note: Reef systems suffer heavily at the end-Guadalupian, a rehearsal for what follows.

biomes.name: Epeiric carbonate platform
biomes.note: Shelf faunas thin out; fusulinids take a severe hit.

biomes.name: Conifer dry woodland
biomes.note: Drought-tolerant gymnosperm woodland across mid-latitude Pangaea.

biomes.name: Dying land surface
biomes.note: The Siberian Traps are erupting through coal and evaporite; forests are collapsing worldwide and soils are washing off the continents in sheets.

biomes.name: Fungal and algal disaster crust
biomes.note: The 'fungal spike' interval -- decay organisms and opportunistic microbes on a landscape stripped of its vegetation.

biomes.name: Anoxic and euxinic ocean
biomes.note: Anoxia spreads from the deep sea onto the shelves; hydrogen sulphide reaches the photic zone in places.

biomes.name: Acidified shallow sea
biomes.note: Rapid CO2 injection acidifies surface water and dissolves the carbonate skeletons the shelf ecosystem is built from.

biomes.name: Collapsing reef system
biomes.note: Every metazoan reef on Earth ceases to exist; there will be no reefs at all for millions of years.

biomes.name: Hyperarid desert
biomes.note: The most complete biome collapse in the plant fossil record, and the start of a ten-million-year coal gap.

biomes.name: Hyperarid desert and lycopod scrub
biomes.note: The coal gap: no peat-forming plants exist anywhere on Earth. Vegetation is low, weedy and dominated by the lycopod Pleuromeia.

biomes.name: Sheetflood alluvial plain
biomes.note: With deep-rooted vegetation gone, rivers revert to braided sheets -- the Devonian channel revolution partly undone.

biomes.name: Anoxic shelf sea
biomes.note: Repeated anoxic pulses through the Early Triassic keep suppressing recovery.

biomes.name: Microbialite seafloor
biomes.note: Stromatolites and microbial mats bloom on the shelves for the first time since the Precambrian, in an ocean with no reef-builders left.

biomes.name: Disaster-fauna shelf
biomes.note: Low-diversity communities dominated by the bivalve Claraia and the brachiopod Lingula -- opportunists in an empty sea.

biomes.name: Hot-tropics dead zone
biomes.note: Equatorial sea-surface temperatures near forty degrees; the tropics are too hot for large animals and are largely abandoned.

biomes.name: Dicroidium seed-fern woodland
biomes.note: The characteristic Gondwanan Triassic forest, and evidence the coal gap is finally over.

biomes.name: Conifer forest
biomes.note: Voltzialean and araucarian conifers rebuild forest structure across both hemispheres.

biomes.name: Megamonsoon desert
biomes.note: Pangaea's size drives an extreme seasonal monsoon: torrential wet seasons alternating with total drought over an enormous arid interior.

biomes.name: Scleractinian reef
biomes.note: Modern-style stone corals appear and start building reefs -- the reef gap closes at last.

biomes.name: Tethyan carbonate platform
biomes.note: The Tethyan embayment becomes the great warm-water carbonate factory of the Mesozoic.

biomes.name: Freshwater temnospondyl swamp
biomes.note: Large amphibians hold the aquatic predator niche in rivers and lakes while reptiles take the land.

biomes.name: Conifer forest
biomes.note: Araucarian and podocarp forest; the Petrified Forest logs are accumulating in Chinle rivers right now.

biomes.name: Megamonsoon desert and erg
biomes.note: Aridity is extreme across Pangaea's interior, punctuated by the Carnian Pluvial Episode's abrupt wet interval.

biomes.name: Cycad and bennettitalean scrub
biomes.note: Stiff, palm-like gymnosperm shrubland forming the understorey across much of the tropics.

biomes.name: Scleractinian reef
biomes.note: Coral reefs expand through the Tethys, joined by sponge and algal builders.

biomes.name: Tethyan carbonate platform
biomes.note: Shallow warm shelves ringing the Tethyan gulf, laying the limestones that will become the Alps.

biomes.name: Braided-river floodplain
biomes.note: Seasonal, high-energy river systems with logjams and standing petrified forests.

biomes.name: Conifer forest
biomes.note: Gymnosperm forest dominates as Pangaea begins to split and CAMP volcanism begins.

biomes.name: Megamonsoon desert
biomes.note: Still the largest arid interior on the planet, now cut by the opening Central Atlantic rift.

biomes.name: Scleractinian reef
biomes.note: Reefs collapse at the Triassic-Jurassic boundary as CAMP CO2 acidifies the ocean.

biomes.name: Anoxic black-shale basin
biomes.note: End-Triassic anoxia across the Tethyan and European shelves.

biomes.name: Rift-valley lake
biomes.note: Newark-type rift lakes with cyclic deep and shallow phases and abundant footprints on their margins.

biomes.name: Cycad and fern understorey
biomes.note: A fern spike marks the boundary -- the classic signature of a devastated land flora recolonising.

biomes.name: Conifer forest
biomes.note: Araucarian and cheirolepid forest from the tropics to high latitudes; there are no polar ice caps to stop it.

biomes.name: Fern prairie
biomes.note: Open, low, fern-dominated ground cover filling the role grass will not take up for another 150 million years.

biomes.name: Epeiric shelf sea
biomes.note: Europe is an archipelago in a shallow warm sea; ammonites and marine reptiles are everywhere.

biomes.name: Anoxic black-shale basin
biomes.note: The Toarcian oceanic anoxic event, coincident with Karoo-Ferrar volcanism, lays down the Posidonia and Jet Rock shales.

biomes.name: Scleractinian reef
biomes.note: Coral reefs rebuild and expand through the widening Tethys.

biomes.name: Cycad and bennettitalean woodland
biomes.note: The 'age of cycads' understorey, and the standard food of large herbivorous dinosaurs.

biomes.name: Conifer forest
biomes.note: Vast araucarian and podocarp forest; the Morrison floodplain forests support the largest land animals yet evolved.

biomes.name: Seasonal savanna-like fern plain
biomes.note: Open ground with fern and horsetail cover on seasonally dry floodplains -- structurally like savanna, with no grass in it.

biomes.name: Siliceous sponge reef belt
biomes.note: A ten-thousand-kilometre belt of glass-sponge reefs along the northern Tethys shelf -- the largest bioconstruction known.

biomes.name: Scleractinian reef
biomes.note: Coral-microbial reefs in shallower, warmer water inshore of the sponge belt.

biomes.name: Epeiric shelf sea
biomes.note: High sea level; broad shallow seas across Europe and western North America.

biomes.name: Calcareous nannoplankton ocean
biomes.note: Coccolithophores and planktic foraminifera take over the open ocean, permanently changing where carbonate is deposited.

biomes.name: Conifer forest
biomes.note: Still the dominant forest, but the first angiosperms are about to appear in disturbed streamside ground.

biomes.name: Fern prairie
biomes.note: Open fern and cycadophyte vegetation across seasonally dry interiors.

biomes.name: Epeiric shelf sea
biomes.note: A cool snap and a sea-level fall at the Jurassic-Cretaceous boundary temporarily drains the epeiric seas.

biomes.name: Calcareous nannoplankton ocean
biomes.note: The open ocean is now a carbonate factory in its own right, not just the shelves.

biomes.name: Scleractinian reef
biomes.note: Corals share reef-building with the first rudist bivalves.

biomes.name: Polar deciduous forest
biomes.note: High-latitude forests with a strong light-seasonality adaptation, and no ice anywhere.

biomes.name: Conifer and cycadophyte forest
biomes.note: Gymnosperms still hold the canopy; angiosperms are weedy riparian invaders at this stage.

biomes.name: Angiosperm riparian thicket
biomes.note: Fast-growing flowering plants colonising disturbed riverbanks -- small, herbaceous, and about to take over the world.

biomes.name: Rudist reef
biomes.note: Bizarre cone-shaped bivalves crowd out corals as the principal tropical reef-builder.

biomes.name: Epeiric carbonate platform
biomes.note: Sea level rising toward the Cretaceous maximum; carbonate platforms are enormous.

biomes.name: Anoxic black-shale basin
biomes.note: The Selli and Weissert events; oceanic anoxic events become a recurring feature of the greenhouse Cretaceous.

biomes.name: Polar deciduous forest
biomes.note: Forests at eighty degrees latitude, with dinosaurs living through months of winter darkness.

biomes.name: Angiosperm forest
biomes.note: Flowering plants take the canopy; forest structure, leaf litter and insect faunas all reorganise around them.

biomes.name: Epeiric chalk sea
biomes.note: Sea level at its Phanerozoic maximum. Coccolith ooze accumulates over drowned continents and becomes the chalk of northern Europe.

biomes.name: Rudist reef
biomes.note: Tropical reef tracts built almost entirely by rudists, in water too warm and saline for corals.

biomes.name: Anoxic black-shale basin
biomes.note: OAE 2 at the Cenomanian-Turonian boundary -- the most extensive anoxia of the Mesozoic.

biomes.name: Conifer forest
biomes.note: Still dominant at high latitudes and in cooler uplands.

biomes.name: Polar temperate forest
biomes.note: No ice at either pole; forest reaches within a few degrees of both.

biomes.name: Angiosperm forest
biomes.note: Flowering-plant forest is the standard land cover, with conifers holding cold and poor ground.

biomes.name: Fern spike disturbance ground
biomes.note: Immediately after Chicxulub, ferns blanket the devastated landscape -- the same recovery signature as the end-Triassic.

biomes.name: Epeiric shelf sea
biomes.note: Sea level is falling from its Cretaceous high; the Western Interior Seaway has largely drained.

biomes.name: Collapsing plankton ocean
biomes.note: Calcareous plankton is nearly annihilated at the boundary, shutting down the ocean's carbon pump for hundreds of thousands of years.

biomes.name: Rudist reef
biomes.note: Rudist reefs are destroyed and never return.

biomes.name: Deccan volcanic plateau
biomes.note: Flood basalt covering much of western India, erupting through and around the impact event.

biomes.name: Paratropical rainforest
biomes.note: The PETM: rainforest reaches far into the mid-latitudes and palms grow in the Arctic.

biomes.name: Polar broadleaf forest
biomes.note: Ellesmere Island supports swamp cypress, alligators and primates at eighty degrees north.

biomes.name: Angiosperm forest
biomes.note: Modern plant families are assembling; forest is the global default land cover.

biomes.name: Warm anoxic-tending ocean
biomes.note: Deep water is warm and poorly oxygenated; benthic foraminifera suffer a severe extinction.

biomes.name: Nummulitic carbonate bank
biomes.note: Giant benthic foraminifera build banks across the Tethyan shelf, later quarried for the pyramids.

biomes.name: Acidified surface ocean
biomes.note: Rapid carbon release drops carbonate saturation and dissolves seafloor ooze -- the closest deep-time analogue to modern acidification.

biomes.name: Paratropical rainforest
biomes.note: Still near-global forest cover, though the extreme Eocene warmth is beginning to relax.

biomes.name: Angiosperm forest
biomes.note: Messel and the Green River lake beds preserve this world in extraordinary detail.

biomes.name: Freshwater Azolla wetland
biomes.note: The Arctic Ocean, fresh and stratified, is covered by floating fern blooms whose burial helps draw CO2 down.

biomes.name: Nummulitic carbonate bank
biomes.note: Tethyan shelf carbonates at their most productive.

biomes.name: Mangrove coast
biomes.note: Modern mangrove communities are established along tropical shorelines.

biomes.name: Archaeocete shelf sea
biomes.note: Fully aquatic whales like Basilosaurus dominate warm shallow seas.

biomes.name: Angiosperm forest
biomes.note: The Eocene-Oligocene transition cools and dries the world; closed rainforest retreats toward the tropics.

biomes.name: Open woodland
biomes.note: The first genuinely open-canopy vegetation of the Cenozoic appears in drying mid-latitude interiors.

biomes.name: Continental ice sheet
biomes.note: The East Antarctic ice sheet forms decisively -- the modern icehouse begins here.

biomes.name: Sea ice
biomes.note: Antarctic sea ice appears for the first time in over two hundred million years.

biomes.name: Temperate deciduous forest
biomes.note: Seasonally cold-adapted broadleaf forest expands in the northern mid-latitudes.

biomes.name: Nothofagus cool-temperate forest
biomes.note: Southern beech forest is the characteristic vegetation of the southern high latitudes, including Antarctica -- just barely.

biomes.name: Open woodland and shrubland
biomes.note: Drier, more open vegetation spreads through continental interiors; browsing mammals diversify to match.

biomes.name: Temperate deciduous forest
biomes.note: Well established across the northern continents.

biomes.name: Early C3 grassland
biomes.note: Grasses have existed since the Cretaceous but only now form open grass-dominated habitats, first in South America.

biomes.name: Continental ice sheet
biomes.note: Antarctic ice waxes and wanes; the Northern Hemisphere is still ice-free.

biomes.name: Kelp forest
biomes.note: Cool coastal upwelling zones develop kelp canopies, and with them a new nearshore ecosystem.

biomes.name: Tropical rainforest
biomes.note: Contracted toward the equator but continuous across the wet tropics.

biomes.name: C3 grassland
biomes.note: The Miocene grassland expansion: open, grazed, fire-maintained landscapes on every continent except Antarctica.

biomes.name: Savanna woodland
biomes.note: Scattered trees over continuous grass -- a biome that has never existed before, and it spreads fast.

biomes.name: Temperate deciduous and conifer forest
biomes.note: Forest retreats to wetter ground as grass takes the interiors.

biomes.name: Tropical rainforest
biomes.note: The Miocene Climatic Optimum briefly re-expands the wet tropics.

biomes.name: Continental ice sheet
biomes.note: The East Antarctic ice sheet stabilises into a permanent feature.

biomes.name: Coral reef
biomes.note: Modern reef provinces take shape; the Indo-Pacific becomes the centre of marine diversity.

biomes.name: C4 grassland
biomes.note: C4 photosynthesis expands worldwide between about eight and three million years ago -- a chemical revolution visible in fossil tooth enamel.

biomes.name: Savanna woodland
biomes.note: The African savanna assembles in something like its modern form, and hominins evolve inside it.

biomes.name: Desert
biomes.note: The Sahara, Atacama and central Asian deserts intensify as mountain uplift and cooling dry the interiors.

biomes.name: Temperate forest and steppe
biomes.note: A sharpening gradient from forest to steppe across Eurasia.

biomes.name: Continental ice sheet
biomes.note: Antarctic ice is permanent; Northern Hemisphere glaciation is beginning.

biomes.name: Coral reef
biomes.note: Reef systems near their modern configuration, with the Coral Triangle already the diversity peak.

biomes.name: C4 grassland and savanna
biomes.note: The dominant tropical and subtropical open biome, and the setting for Australopithecus.

biomes.name: Boreal conifer forest
biomes.note: The taiga belt forms as the Northern Hemisphere cools -- a genuinely new biome of the last few million years.

biomes.name: Tundra
biomes.note: Treeless high-latitude vegetation appears for the first time as permanent northern cold takes hold.

biomes.name: Continental ice sheet
biomes.note: Northern Hemisphere ice sheets begin their glacial-interglacial cycling around 2.7 Ma.

biomes.name: Temperate forest and steppe
biomes.note: Repeatedly displaced and reassembled by orbital-scale climate swings.

biomes.name: Tropical rainforest
biomes.note: Amazonia and the Congo are established; the Isthmus of Panama has closed and rerouted the ocean.

biomes.name: Tropical rainforest
biomes.note: The most biodiverse biome on the planet, concentrated in three shrinking blocks.

biomes.name: Boreal conifer forest
biomes.note: The largest continuous forest on Earth by area, ringing the northern continents.

biomes.name: C4 grassland and savanna
biomes.note: Grasslands and savanna cover a quarter of the ice-free land, most of it now converted to pasture and cropland.

biomes.name: Desert and semi-desert
biomes.note: A broad subtropical arid belt in both hemispheres, expanding at its margins.

biomes.name: Tundra and continental ice sheet
biomes.note: Greenland and Antarctica hold ice sheets; tundra rings the Arctic Ocean on permafrost that is now thawing.

biomes.name: Coral reef and open-ocean plankton
biomes.note: Reefs occupy a tiny fraction of the seafloor but hold a quarter of marine species; the open ocean's plankton still runs the carbon cycle.

biomes.name: Anthropogenic cropland and pasture
biomes.note: For the first time a single species' land use is itself a global biome, covering roughly half of habitable land.

biomes.name: Tropical rainforest (projected)
biomes.note: Wet-tropical forest expands poleward as the icehouse relaxes, if it is not first cleared.

biomes.name: C4 grassland and savanna (projected)
biomes.note: Still extensive, but the arid belts shift poleward and grassland follows.

biomes.name: Boreal forest and shrinking tundra (projected)
biomes.note: Treeline moves north; tundra is squeezed against the Arctic coast.

biomes.name: Residual polar ice (projected)
biomes.note: Antarctic ice persists; Greenland's is likely gone, and the northern icehouse is winding down.

biomes.name: East African seaway (projected)
biomes.note: The rift has flooded: a new narrow ocean with young reef systems along its shores.

biomes.name: Coral reef (projected)
biomes.note: Reef provinces reassembled after a bottleneck, in warmer and more acidic water than today.

biomes.name: Subtropical dry woodland (projected)
biomes.note: A warmer, largely ice-free world with wide seasonal-dry belts.

biomes.name: Tropical rainforest (projected)
biomes.note: Broad equatorial forest belt in a world several degrees warmer than the present.

biomes.name: Alpine and orogenic highland (projected)
biomes.note: The Mediterranean has closed; a Himalayan-scale range runs from Iberia to the Caucasus.

biomes.name: Epeiric carbonate platform (projected)
biomes.note: High sea level in an ice-free world floods continental margins and restores broad shallow seas.

biomes.name: Temperate forest (projected)
biomes.note: Pushed to high latitudes, with no tundra beyond it to speak of.

biomes.name: Warm stratified ocean (projected)
biomes.note: Weaker overturning and expanded oxygen minimum zones as the poles warm.

biomes.name: Continental interior desert (projected)
biomes.note: The assembling supercontinent is developing an interior far from any coast -- aridity on the Permian model.

biomes.name: Megamonsoon seasonal forest (projected)
biomes.note: Coastal belts soaked in a monsoon season and parched the rest of the year.

biomes.name: Tropical rainforest (projected)
biomes.note: Confined to windward coasts and equatorial margins.

biomes.name: Collision-belt highland (projected)
biomes.note: Mountain chains along the sutures where the continents are welding together.

biomes.name: Neo-Panthalassic open ocean (projected)
biomes.note: A single vast world-ocean on the far side of the assembling landmass.

biomes.name: Epeiric carbonate platform (projected)
biomes.note: Warm shallow shelves ringing the supercontinent, the main marine habitat.

biomes.name: Hyperarid supercontinental desert (projected)
biomes.note: Pangaea Proxima's interior may be the driest large landscape since the Permian, and hotter -- the Sun is measurably brighter.

biomes.name: Megamonsoon seasonal woodland (projected)
biomes.note: Extreme wet-dry seasonality on the continental margins, as with Pangaea.

biomes.name: Tropical rainforest (projected)
biomes.note: Restricted to a narrow coastal fringe where onshore moisture reaches land.

biomes.name: Warm shelf sea (projected)
biomes.note: A hothouse ocean with high sea level, expanded oxygen minimum zones and reduced overturning.

biomes.name: Anoxic black-shale basin (projected)
biomes.note: Restricted basins along the suturing margins, on the Tethyan model.

biomes.name: Neo-Panthalassic open ocean (projected)
biomes.note: One ocean covering most of the planet, its interior far from any land-derived nutrient supply.

life.summary: Life is entirely microbial and aquatic, but it is not simple. Eukaryotes have been around for a billion years and are now diversifying into recognisable groups -- red algae, green algae, amoebae with shells, and the first fungi. The sea is run by cyanobacteria and small algae, with stromatolite reefs on every warm shelf, and below a thin oxygenated surface layer the water is anoxic and often sulphidic. Land is stone: bare regolith, braided rivers with no banks, and at most a thin microbial and possibly fungal crust on damp surfaces. Nothing anywhere is more than a few millimetres across.

taxa.name: Cyanobacteria
taxa.note: The engine of the whole biosphere: oxygen producers and the builders of stromatolite reefs for well over a billion years.

taxa.name: Bangiomorpha pubescens
taxa.note: A filamentous red alga with differentiated cells and sexual reproduction -- one of the oldest fossils that can be tied to a living group.

taxa.name: Acritarcha
taxa.note: Organic-walled cysts of algae, too poorly understood to classify but abundant enough to date rocks with.

taxa.name: Ourasphaira giraldae
taxa.note: Branching filaments with chitin-like walls from Arctic Canada, and the strongest candidate for the oldest fungus.

taxa.name: Arcellinida
taxa.note: Vase-shaped microfossils -- testate amoebae that built shells and, by implication, had something to hide from.

taxa.name: Chlorophyta
taxa.note: Green algae established in shallow water; the ancestors of every land plant are somewhere in this group.

extinctions: Long decline of stromatolite abundance and diversity
Turnover of Mesoproterozoic acritarch assemblages

life.summary: Two global glaciations -- the Sturtian and the Marinoan -- freeze the ocean surface to near-tropical latitudes, with a genuinely non-glacial interval of several million years between them. The marine biosphere is sealed under ice for long stretches and survives, probably in cryoconite meltponds on the ice surface and in narrow open-water bands near the equator. Eukaryotic diversity drops hard and then rebounds after each thaw, and the survivors emerge into a world with far more oxygen than before. Iron formations reappear after a billion-year absence because the sub-ice ocean has nowhere to dump its dissolved iron. Land, under ice, is scoured rock.

taxa.name: Cyanobacteria
taxa.note: Survive the freeze in refugia; every recovery is built on them.

taxa.name: Chlorophyta
taxa.note: Green algae pass through both snowballs and diversify sharply afterwards.

taxa.name: Acritarcha
taxa.note: Diversity collapses at each glacial onset and recovers with a different cast each time.

taxa.name: Porifera
taxa.note: Molecular clocks and disputed biomarkers place sponges here; unambiguous body fossils come later.

taxa.name: Bacteria
taxa.note: Chemosynthetic and heterotrophic communities in the sub-ice ocean, running on whatever the ice lets through.

taxa.name: Rhodophyta
taxa.note: Red algae persist through the glaciations in shallow refugia.

first_appearances: Probable earliest sponges (molecular and biomarker evidence)
extinctions: Severe loss of acritarch diversity at both glacial onsets
Widespread collapse of stromatolite ecosystems during the freezes

life.summary: In the aftermath of the Marinoan, oxygen rises and large, soft-bodied, multicellular organisms appear -- the Ediacaran biota, the first macroscopic life on Earth. Some are fractal fronds standing in the deep sea below the reach of light, feeding on dissolved organic matter; others lie flat on microbial mats in shallow water. The seafloor is still a sealed mat surface because almost nothing burrows, and that changes only at the very end of the period. Right at the close, Cloudina builds the first mineralised skeletons and the first animal reefs, and the first predatory borings appear in them. Land remains lifeless above the microbial crust.

taxa.name: Ediacaran biota
taxa.note: A grab-bag of frondose, discoid and quilted organisms whose relationships to living animals are still argued about a century after their discovery.

taxa.name: Rangeomorpha
taxa.note: Fractal, self-similar fronds anchored in deep water at Mistaken Point -- a body plan with no modern counterpart.

taxa.name: Dickinsonia
taxa.note: A flat, segmented, centimetre-to-metre oval that left feeding traces as it moved; cholesterol in its tissues shows it was an animal.

taxa.name: Kimberella
taxa.note: A bilaterally symmetrical grazer that scraped mats with a feeding structure -- the best candidate for an early mollusc relative.

taxa.name: Cloudina
taxa.note: Stacked calcareous cones that built the first animal reefs, and carry the first drill holes made by a predator.

taxa.name: Namacalathus
taxa.note: A goblet-shaped skeletal organism from the Nama Group, part of the first mineralised reef community.

taxa.name: Charnia masoni
taxa.note: The frond from Charnwood Forest that proved Precambrian rocks contain complex life.

first_appearances: Bilaterian body plans (trace and body fossil evidence)
extinctions: Near-total disappearance of the Ediacaran frondose biota at the end of the period
Collapse of the mat-bound seafloor ecosystem as burrowing begins

life.summary: Almost every animal phylum with a fossil record appears within a few tens of millions of years. Skeletons, eyes, guts, limbs and predation all become widespread at once, and the seafloor is churned by burrowers for the first time, permanently ending the Precambrian mat world. Archaeocyath sponges build the first framework reefs, then vanish before the period is half over. Chordates are present from early on but are small and unremarkable -- Haikouichthys is a finger-length swimmer in a sea ruled by arthropods. Land stays bare rock throughout; the entire event is marine.

taxa.name: Trilobita
taxa.note: The defining Cambrian arthropod: armoured, mobile, with compound eyes made of calcite crystals.

taxa.name: Anomalocaris
taxa.note: A metre-long swimming predator with grasping appendages, and the first animal large enough to sit at the top of a food web.

taxa.name: Archaeocyatha
taxa.note: Sponge-grade cone-shaped reef builders that made the first animal reef framework and were extinct within twenty million years.

taxa.name: Haikouichthys ercaicunensis
taxa.note: A tiny Chengjiang swimmer with a notochord and rudimentary vertebrae -- an early member of our own lineage.

taxa.name: Hallucigenia
taxa.note: A spined, stilt-legged lobopodian reconstructed upside-down and backwards for decades before anyone got it right.

taxa.name: Wiwaxia
taxa.note: A scale-covered mat grazer whose affinities have been argued between molluscs and annelids for a century.

taxa.name: Brachiopoda
taxa.note: Shelled filter feeders that will dominate the shelf benthos for the next three hundred million years.

taxa.name: Conodonta
taxa.note: Eel-like chordates known mostly from their tooth elements, which become the finest stratigraphic tool in the Palaeozoic.

extinctions: Archaeocyaths (end of the Early Cambrian)
Repeated Cambrian trilobite biomere extinctions
Loss of much of the Ediacaran holdover fauna

life.summary: The Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event begins: marine diversity roughly triples over the period, with the increase coming from stacking more animals into more niches rather than inventing new body plans. Filter feeders build up off the seafloor in tiers, and graptolites colonise the open water column permanently. Reefs are still mostly microbial and sponge-built, because the archaeocyaths are gone and corals have not yet taken over. Fish remain small, jawless and armoured. The first land plants -- liverwort-grade, non-vascular, a few millimetres tall -- appear as spores toward the end of this interval.

taxa.name: Graptolithina
taxa.note: Colonial hemichordates drifting in open water, whose fast turnover makes them the timekeepers of the Ordovician.

taxa.name: Nautiloidea
taxa.note: Straight-shelled cephalopods, some several metres long, and the top predators of the Early Palaeozoic sea.

taxa.name: Trilobita
taxa.note: Still abundant and now diversifying into deep-water, planktic and specialised burrowing forms.

taxa.name: Brachiopoda
taxa.note: Articulate brachiopods explode in diversity and take over the shelf benthos.

taxa.name: Conodonta
taxa.note: Diversifying rapidly; conodont elements are how this interval's rocks are actually dated.

taxa.name: Marchantiophyta
taxa.note: Liverwort-grade plants -- the first land vegetation, known from cryptospores rather than bodies.

taxa.name: Ostracoda
taxa.note: Tiny bivalved crustaceans that become one of the most continuous fossil records of the entire Phanerozoic.

extinctions: Late Cambrian biomere extinctions taper off
Turnover of Cambrian-type trilobite faunas

life.summary: Diversification hits its peak rate. Bryozoans, crinoids, articulate brachiopods, rugose and tabulate corals and stromatoporoid sponges assemble into the Palaeozoic Evolutionary Fauna, and reefs become large, structured and recognisably reef-like for the first time. Crinoid meadows are dense enough that their broken stems make the rock. Nautiloids remain the top predators and reach enormous sizes. On land, cryptogamic ground cover spreads across damp low ground, still without vascular tissue or roots.

taxa.name: Crinoidea
taxa.note: Stalked echinoderms in meadows so dense that entire limestone formations are made of their debris.

taxa.name: Bryozoa
taxa.note: Colonial encrusters and branching forms that build much of the reef and hardground framework.

taxa.name: Tabulata
taxa.note: Colonial corals with honeycomb skeletons, joining stromatoporoids as reef builders.

taxa.name: Stromatoporoidea
taxa.note: Calcified sponges that are the principal reef framework builders of the Middle Palaeozoic.

taxa.name: Cameroceras
taxa.note: A giant straight-shelled nautiloid, possibly six metres long, hunting the shelf seas.

taxa.name: Ostracoderms
taxa.note: Jawless armoured fish, bottom-feeding and slow, and the only vertebrates in the water.

taxa.name: Marchantiophyta
taxa.note: Ground-hugging non-vascular plants forming the first continuous, if thin, land cover.

extinctions: Progressive replacement of Cambrian-type faunas by the Palaeozoic Fauna

life.summary: Diversity reaches an early Palaeozoic maximum and is then cut down by the first of the big five mass extinctions. Gondwana drifts over the South Pole, an ice sheet grows across what is now the Sahara, and sea level drops by a hundred metres or more, draining the epeiric seas where most marine life lived. A cold-water, low-diversity Hirnantia brachiopod fauna spreads worldwide; then the ice melts, anoxic water floods back onto the shelves, and a second pulse kills much of what survived the first. Around eighty-five percent of species are lost. Land plants come through it more or less intact.

taxa.name: Hirnantia
taxa.note: The name-bearer of the cold-water brachiopod fauna that briefly took over the world's shelves during the glaciation.

taxa.name: Graptolithina
taxa.note: Devastated: most graptolite lineages are wiped out in the two extinction pulses.

taxa.name: Trilobita
taxa.note: Loses many families permanently and never regains its Ordovician diversity.

taxa.name: Crinoidea
taxa.note: Heavy losses, followed by a Silurian rebound into new forms.

taxa.name: Conodonta
taxa.note: Severe extinction, and the recovery fauna looks entirely different.

taxa.name: Tabulata
taxa.note: Reef systems collapse with the sea-level fall and take millions of years to rebuild.

taxa.name: Marchantiophyta
taxa.note: Bryophyte-grade land cover, and one hypothesis for why the ice came at all -- plant-driven weathering pulling CO2 down.

extinctions: End-Ordovician mass extinction: roughly 85% of species
Most graptolite lineages
Many trilobite, brachiopod and conodont families
Widespread reef collapse

life.summary: Recovery is fast. Sea level rebounds, epeiric seas return, and reef systems rebuild into one of the great reef intervals of the Palaeozoic -- Gotland and the Michigan Basin pinnacle reefs are Silurian. Jawed fish appear and start to matter, and eurypterids up to two metres long dominate restricted brackish and hypersaline basins. On land, the decisive event is vascular tissue: Cooksonia and its relatives are leafless, rootless stems a few centimetres tall, but they can conduct water and stand upright, and everything terrestrial follows from that. The first land arthropods -- millipedes and arachnid relatives -- come ashore with them.

taxa.name: Cooksonia
taxa.note: A few centimetres of leafless forking stem with a spore capsule on top: the first vascular plant, and the ancestor of every forest.

taxa.name: Eurypterus
taxa.note: Sea scorpions patrolling brackish lagoons, some large enough to take vertebrate prey.

taxa.name: Acanthodii
taxa.note: Spiny 'sharks' -- among the earliest jawed fish, and the point where vertebrates start eating things that fight back.

taxa.name: Halysites
taxa.note: Chain coral, a diagnostic Silurian reef builder whose colonies form linked palisades.

taxa.name: Pterygotus
taxa.note: A giant eurypterid with grasping claws, one of the largest arthropods that ever lived.

taxa.name: Myriapoda
taxa.note: Millipede-grade arthropods, among the first animals to live permanently out of water.

taxa.name: Baragwanathia
taxa.note: A lycophyte with real leaves, appearing surprisingly early in Australia and complicating every tidy story about plant evolution.

taxa.name: Ostracoderms
taxa.note: Jawless armoured fish now common in fresh water as well as the sea.

extinctions: Multiple Silurian oceanic anoxic events (Ireviken, Mulde, Lau) with heavy graptolite and conodont losses

life.summary: Land vegetation gets structure. Zosterophylls and trimerophytes spread by rhizome into knee-high thickets, and the Rhynie chert -- a hot-spring deposit that silicified a whole wetland in growth position -- preserves plants, mites, springtails, a trigonotarbid arachnid and the oldest known insect, all in cellular detail. In the water this is the Age of Fishes proper: placoderms armoured in bone plates, acanthodians, early sharks and lobe-finned fish all diversify at once. Reefs reach their greatest extent of the entire Palaeozoic, built by stromatoporoids and tabulate corals. Rivers begin to meander, because plant roots finally make banks that hold.

taxa.name: Rhynia
taxa.note: A leafless, rootless Rhynie chert plant preserved cell by cell, and the closest thing we have to a photograph of the first land ecosystem.

taxa.name: Placodermi
taxa.note: Jawed fish encased in articulated bony armour; for sixty million years they run the seas, then vanish completely.

taxa.name: Rhyniognatha hirsti
taxa.note: A pair of mandibles from the Rhynie chert, and the oldest fossil generally accepted as an insect.

taxa.name: Trigonotarbida
taxa.note: Spider-like arachnids among the first land predators -- there was already something worth hunting.

taxa.name: Zosterophyllopsida
taxa.note: Sprawling, rhizomatous vascular plants that built the first vegetation dense enough to change how rivers behave.

taxa.name: Osteichthyes
taxa.note: Bony fish split into ray-fins and lobe-fins here; one of those branches leads to everything with four limbs.

taxa.name: Stromatoporoidea
taxa.note: Reef builders at their all-time peak; Devonian reef tracts exceed the modern reef belt in area.

extinctions: Basal Zlichov and other Early Devonian anoxic events with ammonoid and trilobite losses

life.summary: Trees are invented. Cladoxylopsids like Wattieza at Gilboa form the first stands of tree-sized plants, and progymnosperms follow with real wood. For the first time in Earth's history something casts shade, drops litter, and pushes roots a metre into the substrate, which transforms weathering, soil and river chemistry. Fish diversity peaks: giant placoderms like Dunkleosteus reach six metres with shearing bony jaws. The lobe-finned fish that will become tetrapods are living in shallow, vegetated, oxygen-poor water where breathing air is an advantage.

taxa.name: Wattieza
taxa.note: The Gilboa tree: a trunk topped by a frond crown, and the oldest known forest stand.

taxa.name: Archaeopteris
taxa.note: The first plant with a woody trunk and a true leafy canopy -- effectively the first modern-looking tree.

taxa.name: Dunkleosteus
taxa.note: A six-metre placoderm that sheared prey with self-sharpening bony blades instead of teeth.

taxa.name: Eusthenopteron
taxa.note: A lobe-finned fish with the limb bone arrangement of a tetrapod already inside its fin.

taxa.name: Ammonoidea
taxa.note: Coiled cephalopods diversifying fast; they will become the single best index fossil of the Mesozoic.

taxa.name: Progymnospermopsida
taxa.note: Wood-producing plants that still reproduce by spores -- the structural revolution before the reproductive one.

taxa.name: Chondrichthyes
taxa.note: Early sharks spreading through marine and freshwater habitats.

extinctions: Taghanic event: major loss of endemic brachiopod and coral provinces

life.summary: Vertebrates walk out of the water. Tiktaalik, Acanthostega and Ichthyostega document the fin-to-limb transition in a few million years of rock, though these animals are still aquatic and use limbs for moving through weedy shallows rather than crossing land. Meanwhile forests spread worldwide, pull CO2 down and pour nutrients into the sea, and the shelves suffer the drawn-out Frasnian-Famennian crisis: repeated anoxic events that destroy the stromatoporoid-coral reef ecosystem so thoroughly it is not rebuilt at that scale for a hundred million years. The Hangenberg event at the very end of the period finishes off the placoderms entirely. Seed plants appear, freeing reproduction from standing water.

taxa.name: Tiktaalik roseae
taxa.note: A flat-headed predator with a neck, wrists and lungs, found in Arctic Canada exactly where and when the rocks predicted it would be.

taxa.name: Acanthostega
taxa.note: An early tetrapod with eight fingers and internal gills -- limbs evolved in the water, not for walking on land.

taxa.name: Ichthyostega
taxa.note: A more robust tetrapod from East Greenland, able to haul itself but still tied to water.

taxa.name: Archaeopteris
taxa.note: Forms the world's first widespread forests, and is implicated in the extinction that follows.

taxa.name: Hyneria
taxa.note: A large predatory lobe-fin hunting in the same rivers as the first tetrapods, and eating them.

taxa.name: Placodermi
taxa.note: Wiped out completely at the Hangenberg event -- an entire class of vertebrates gone in a geological instant.

taxa.name: Elkinsia
taxa.note: One of the earliest seed plants; the seed is what eventually lets vegetation leave the water's edge.

taxa.name: Bothriolepis
taxa.note: An antiarch placoderm so abundant and widespread it is effectively the index fossil of Devonian fresh water.

extinctions: Frasnian-Famennian (Kellwasser) extinction: reef ecosystems destroyed
Hangenberg event: placoderms eliminated entirely
Severe losses among trilobites, ammonoids and jawless fish

life.summary: The sea belongs to crinoids -- meadows dense enough that entire limestone formations are made of their shattered stems -- and to sharks, which radiate spectacularly into the space placoderms left. On land there is a genuine gap in the record: Romer's Gap, roughly twenty million years where tetrapods must be diversifying but are barely fossilised. When the record resumes at East Kirkton and Bear Gulch, tetrapods have already split toward amphibian and amniote lineages and Westlothiana is walking around on dry ground. Peat accumulation begins in earnest as coastal mires spread, and ice starts building over high-latitude Gondwana.

taxa.name: Crinoidea
taxa.note: The Mississippian is the crinoid's high-water mark; the Burlington Limestone is essentially compacted echinoderm.

taxa.name: Chondrichthyes
taxa.note: Sharks and their relatives explode into bizarre forms, including tooth-whorled Helicoprion's ancestors.

taxa.name: Westlothiana lizziae
taxa.note: A small, slender East Kirkton tetrapod, close to the origin of fully terrestrial amniotes.

taxa.name: Blastoidea
taxa.note: Bud-shaped echinoderms, abundant now and destined to disappear at the end of the Permian.

taxa.name: Lepidodendrales
taxa.note: Scale trees beginning their takeover of coastal mires -- the coal machine is warming up.

taxa.name: Rhizodus
taxa.note: A seven-metre freshwater lobe-finned predator, the largest freshwater fish known.

taxa.name: Foraminifera
taxa.note: Larger benthic forams diversify and become key shelf-carbonate contributors.

extinctions: Serpukhovian crisis: heavy crinoid and ammonoid losses as Gondwanan glaciation intensifies

life.summary: The coal forests. Waterlogged equatorial mires filled with thirty-metre lycopsids, tree ferns, calamiteans and seed ferns bury organic carbon faster than any biome before or since, and nearly all the world's coal is made here. Oxygen climbs above thirty percent, which permits insects at sizes physically impossible today: Meganeura with a seventy-centimetre wingspan, and Arthropleura, a two-metre millipede. Amniotes appear -- Hylonomus in the hollow stumps at Joggins -- and with the amniotic egg, vertebrates finally cut the last tie to standing water. Toward the end of the interval the Carboniferous Rainforest Collapse fragments the swamp into refugia and drives tetrapod faunas into isolation.

taxa.name: Lepidodendron
taxa.note: A thirty-metre lycopsid that grew fast, reproduced once and toppled -- the principal ingredient of coal.

taxa.name: Meganeura
taxa.note: A dragonfly relative with a wingspan approaching three-quarters of a metre, possible only in a high-oxygen atmosphere.

taxa.name: Arthropleura
taxa.note: A two-metre millipede, the largest land arthropod that has ever existed, leaving trackways across swamp floors.

taxa.name: Hylonomus lyelli
taxa.note: A lizard-shaped animal found inside fossil tree stumps at Joggins, and the earliest well-established amniote.

taxa.name: Calamites
taxa.note: Tree-sized horsetails forming dense stands along channel margins.

taxa.name: Medullosales
taxa.note: Seed ferns with enormous fronds and the largest seeds of the Palaeozoic.

taxa.name: Tullimonstrum gregarium
taxa.note: The Mazon Creek 'Tully monster' -- eyes on a bar, jaws on a proboscis, and no settled classification.

taxa.name: Edaphosaurus
taxa.note: An early sail-backed synapsid, and one of the first large herbivorous land vertebrates.

extinctions: Carboniferous Rainforest Collapse: fragmentation of the tropical everwet flora and severe tetrapod turnover

life.summary: Pangaea is assembled and its interior is enormous, continental and dry. The coal swamps retreat, conifers and other drought-tolerant seed plants take the uplands, and Glossopteris spreads across deglaciating Gondwana as a genuinely seasonal high-latitude forest. On land the dominant large vertebrates are synapsids -- our own lineage -- with Dimetrodon at the top of the food chain and Eryops and other big temnospondyl amphibians in the water. Oxygen is still very high and then begins a long decline. In the sea, bryozoan-sponge-algal reefs like the Capitan build up on the shelf margins, and fusulinid foraminifera become the dominant carbonate producers.

taxa.name: Dimetrodon
taxa.note: A sail-backed synapsid predator, more closely related to us than to any dinosaur, and routinely mis-sold as one.

taxa.name: Glossopteris
taxa.note: A tongue-leaved seed fern blanketing Gondwana, whose distribution across five now-separate continents was early evidence for continental drift.

taxa.name: Eryops
taxa.note: A heavy-bodied temnospondyl amphibian, effectively the crocodile of Permian rivers.

taxa.name: Fusulinida
taxa.note: Rice-grain-sized foraminifera so abundant they make limestone, and so fast-evolving they date it.

taxa.name: Seymouria
taxa.note: A tetrapod so close to the amphibian-amniote boundary that its placement has flipped repeatedly.

taxa.name: Helicoprion
taxa.note: A shark relative with a buzzsaw whorl of teeth in its lower jaw, whose function took a century to work out.

taxa.name: Walchia
taxa.note: An early conifer in drier upland settings -- the beginning of forest that is not a swamp.

extinctions: Olson's Extinction: substantial turnover of terrestrial tetrapod faunas
Continued decline of Carboniferous swamp flora

life.summary: Therapsids take over the land completely. Dinocephalians, dicynodonts and the first gorgonopsians produce large herbivores and large predators with increasingly upright limbs and differentiated teeth, and the Karoo Basin records the sequence in detail. The Cathaysian flora persists as an isolated wet-tropical refuge on the Chinese blocks, with Gigantopteris and its enormous leaves. Marine shelves are rich, with fusulinids, brachiopods and sponge-algal reefs. At the end of the interval the Emeishan Traps erupt in South China and the end-Guadalupian extinction removes much of the reef and fusulinid fauna -- a rehearsal for what is eight million years away.

taxa.name: Dicynodontia
taxa.note: Beaked, tusked herbivorous therapsids that become the most abundant large land animals on Earth.

taxa.name: Gorgonopsia
taxa.note: Sabre-toothed therapsid predators with an erect gait -- the first mammal-line animals that hunt like mammals.

taxa.name: Dinocephalia
taxa.note: Massive, thick-skulled therapsids, likely head-butting, that go extinct at the end of the interval.

taxa.name: Gigantopteris
taxa.note: A Cathaysian seed plant with broad net-veined leaves that look startlingly like an angiosperm's, 150 million years early.

taxa.name: Fusulinida
taxa.note: Reaches its greatest size and diversity, then is severely culled at the end-Guadalupian.

taxa.name: Productida
taxa.note: Spiny, cemented brachiopods that dominate Permian shelf benthos.

taxa.name: Glossopteris
taxa.note: Still the dominant Gondwanan forest tree, laying down the coal of Australia, India and Antarctica.

extinctions: End-Guadalupian (Capitanian) extinction: dinocephalians lost, fusulinids and reefs heavily hit
Emeishan-linked losses in South China

life.summary: A rich, complex world ends abruptly. Dicynodonts and gorgonopsians dominate a land covered in Glossopteris forest and conifer woodland; the sea holds diverse brachiopods, crinoids, bryozoans, fusulinids and sponge-algal reefs. Then the Siberian Traps erupt through coal and evaporite, and the end-Permian extinction removes something like ninety-six percent of marine species and seventy percent of terrestrial vertebrate genera. Every peat-forming plant lineage goes extinct, producing a ten-million-year global coal gap, and the sea loses trilobites, blastoids, rugose and tabulate corals and eurypterids permanently. It is the closest complex life has come to being erased.

taxa.name: Inostrancevia
taxa.note: A bear-sized gorgonopsian with sabre teeth, the apex predator of the last Permian ecosystems.

taxa.name: Dicynodon
taxa.note: An abundant tusked herbivore whose disappearance defines the terrestrial extinction horizon in the Karoo.

taxa.name: Trilobita
taxa.note: After 270 million years and thousands of species, the group ends here.

taxa.name: Rugosa
taxa.note: Solitary and colonial Palaeozoic corals, extinguished entirely; the corals that follow are a different lineage.

taxa.name: Blastoidea
taxa.note: Bud-shaped echinoderms wiped out completely at the boundary.

taxa.name: Glossopteris
taxa.note: The great Gondwanan forest flora ends here, and no peat forms anywhere on Earth for millions of years.

taxa.name: Eurypterida
taxa.note: Sea scorpions, in decline for a hundred million years, finally gone.

taxa.name: Lystrosaurus
taxa.note: A pig-sized dicynodont that survives the extinction and then makes up most of the land vertebrate fauna of the entire planet.

first_appearances: Survivor-lineage cynodonts and archosauromorphs positioned to inherit the Triassic
extinctions: End-Permian mass extinction: ~96% of marine species, ~70% of terrestrial vertebrate genera
Trilobites
Rugose and tabulate corals
Blastoids
Eurypterids
Fusulinids
All peat-forming plant lineages (the coal gap)

life.summary: A depleted, strange world. Land vegetation is low, weedy lycopod scrub -- Pleuromeia -- with no peat-formers anywhere, and with deep-rooted plants gone the rivers revert to braided sheetflood systems. Lystrosaurus is so dominant that at some Karoo horizons it accounts for most vertebrate fossils on the planet. The sea has no reef builders at all, so microbial mats and stromatolites bloom on the shelves for the first time since the Precambrian, and low-diversity disaster taxa like the bivalve Claraia carpet the seafloor. Equatorial sea-surface temperatures reach the high thirties and the tropics are largely abandoned by large animals. Recovery is repeatedly knocked back by further anoxic pulses.

taxa.name: Lystrosaurus
taxa.note: The survivor: a stocky dicynodont so abundant after the extinction it is effectively the only large land animal in the fossil record.

taxa.name: Claraia
taxa.note: A thin-shelled bivalve that carpets post-extinction seafloors -- the classic disaster taxon.

taxa.name: Pleuromeia
taxa.note: A metre-tall unbranched lycopod that stands in for an entire vanished forest flora.

taxa.name: Proterosuchus
taxa.note: An early archosaur, sprawling and crocodile-like, at the root of the lineage that will produce dinosaurs and birds.

taxa.name: Chaohusaurus
taxa.note: One of the earliest ichthyosaurs: within a few million years of the extinction, reptiles are already back in the sea.

taxa.name: Cyanobacteria
taxa.note: Microbialites and stromatolites bloom on shelves emptied of skeletal reef builders.

taxa.name: Lingula
taxa.note: A burrowing brachiopod that survives everything and looks much the same today.

extinctions: Smithian-Spathian crisis: further losses that delay recovery
Repeated Early Triassic anoxic events

life.summary: Recovery finally takes hold. Scleractinian corals -- an entirely new lineage, not descended from the Palaeozoic reef builders -- appear and start building reefs again, closing the reef gap. The sea fills with marine reptiles: ichthyosaurs, nothosaurs, placodonts crushing shellfish, and the first plesiosaur relatives, preserved spectacularly in the Luoping and Panxian faunas of South China. On land, archosaurs diversify into rauisuchians and the first dinosauromorphs while cynodonts edge toward mammals. The coal gap closes as Dicroidium seed-fern woodland spreads across Gondwana. Ammonoids, nearly extinguished, rebound explosively and become the timekeepers of the Mesozoic.

taxa.name: Scleractinia
taxa.note: Stone corals appear from nowhere and rebuild the reef ecosystem the Permian destroyed; every modern reef descends from them.

taxa.name: Nothosaurus
taxa.note: A long-necked, semi-aquatic fish-catcher representing an early stage of the sauropterygian move into the sea.

taxa.name: Placodontia
taxa.note: Marine reptiles with flat crushing teeth and, in some, turtle-like armour, specialised on shellfish.

taxa.name: Dicroidium
taxa.note: The forked-leaf seed fern that defines Gondwanan Triassic forest and marks the end of the coal gap.

taxa.name: Cynognathus
taxa.note: A dog-sized cynodont with differentiated teeth and probably fur -- most of the way to a mammal.

taxa.name: Ammonoidea
taxa.note: Squeezed through a bottleneck of a handful of lineages, then radiating into thousands of species.

taxa.name: Tanystropheus
taxa.note: A reptile whose neck is longer than the rest of it combined, with only twelve vertebrae in it.

extinctions: Ladinian turnover of early Triassic recovery faunas

life.summary: Dinosaurs appear -- and for most of this interval they are a minor component, outnumbered and outsized by rauisuchian and phytosaur pseudosuchians. The Carnian Pluvial Episode, an abrupt wet interval likely tied to Wrangellia volcanism, restructures floras and coincides with the dinosaur radiation. Mammals originate as shrew-sized nocturnal insectivores. Pterosaurs take to the air, the first vertebrates to fly under power. Conifer forest and cycadophyte scrub cover the land, with a vast megamonsoonal desert in Pangaea's interior. The interval ends with CAMP volcanism, ocean acidification and the end-Triassic extinction, which removes the dinosaurs' competitors and hands them the Jurassic.

taxa.name: Coelophysis bauri
taxa.note: A slender early theropod known from hundreds of individuals at Ghost Ranch, piled up in a single mass death assemblage.

taxa.name: Plateosaurus
taxa.note: An early long-necked sauropodomorph, and among the first genuinely large herbivorous dinosaurs.

taxa.name: Morganucodon
taxa.note: A shrew-sized nocturnal insectivore with a mammalian jaw joint -- close to the origin of mammals.

taxa.name: Eudimorphodon
taxa.note: An early pterosaur with a complex tooth battery, already fully capable of powered flight.

taxa.name: Postosuchus
taxa.note: A large pseudosuchian predator that outranked every dinosaur of its day, and died out at the boundary.

taxa.name: Shonisaurus
taxa.note: A giant ichthyosaur reaching twenty metres, comparable to a modern large whale.

taxa.name: Araucarioxylon
taxa.note: The conifer whose logs make the Petrified Forest, transported and buried in seasonal river systems.

taxa.name: Conodonta
taxa.note: After 300 million years as the best index fossil in the Palaeozoic, conodonts end at the close of the Triassic.

extinctions: End-Triassic mass extinction (~201.4 Ma), linked to CAMP volcanism
Conodonts
Most rauisuchians and phytosaurs
Heavy ammonoid and reef losses

life.summary: With their competitors gone, dinosaurs take over completely: sauropodomorphs get big, theropods diversify, and armoured thyreophorans like Scelidosaurus appear. The seas around a flooded, archipelago-like Europe are extraordinarily well recorded -- the Blue Lias at Lyme Regis and the Posidonia Shale at Holzmaden preserve ichthyosaurs with skin outlines and unborn young, plesiosaurs, and ammonites in the millions. The Toarcian oceanic anoxic event, coincident with Karoo-Ferrar volcanism, lays down black shales across the northern shelves and causes a substantial marine extinction. Forests are araucarian and podocarp conifer with fern ground cover; there is no grass and no flower anywhere.

taxa.name: Ichthyosaurus
taxa.note: Streamlined, live-bearing marine reptiles; Mary Anning's Lyme Regis specimens are how the world learned they existed.

taxa.name: Plesiosaurus
taxa.note: Long-necked, four-flippered marine reptiles rowing through shallow Jurassic seas.

taxa.name: Dilophosaurus
taxa.note: A crested early theropod, six metres long and nothing like its film portrayal.

taxa.name: Scelidosaurus
taxa.note: An early armoured dinosaur, at the base of the lineage leading to stegosaurs and ankylosaurs.

taxa.name: Ammonoidea
taxa.note: So abundant and fast-evolving that Jurassic time is subdivided by ammonite zones a few hundred thousand years long.

taxa.name: Cryolophosaurus ellioti
taxa.note: A crested theropod from the Transantarctic Mountains, showing dinosaurs living at high southern latitudes.

taxa.name: Belemnitida
