taxa.note: Squid-like cephalopods whose bullet-shaped guards are among the commonest Jurassic fossils.

extinctions: Toarcian oceanic anoxic event: substantial marine invertebrate extinction
Loss of several early Jurassic ammonite lineages

life.summary: A poorly exposed but pivotal interval: sauropods become genuinely gigantic, theropods split into the lineages that will produce tyrannosaurs, allosaurs and maniraptorans, and the first feathered dinosaurs appear. Mammals diversify into gliding, swimming and digging forms rather than remaining generic insectivores. In the sea, coccolithophores and planktic foraminifera take over the open ocean and permanently change where carbonate is deposited -- carbonate stops being purely a shelf phenomenon. Pangaea is splitting, and the widening seaways begin isolating faunas from each other.

taxa.name: Megalosaurus
taxa.note: The first dinosaur ever formally named, from Oxfordshire, decades before anyone had the concept of a dinosaur.

taxa.name: Castorocauda lutrasimilis
taxa.note: A beaver-tailed, swimming mammaliaform with preserved fur -- evidence Jurassic mammals were not all generic shrews.

taxa.name: Volaticotherium
taxa.note: A gliding mammaliaform with a preserved membrane, roughly 100 million years before bats.

taxa.name: Coccolithophyceae
taxa.note: Microscopic plated algae that take over the open ocean and start building chalk.

taxa.name: Cetiosaurus
taxa.note: An early large sauropod, originally mistaken for a giant marine reptile.

taxa.name: Anchiornis
taxa.note: A small feathered paravian preserved well enough for its actual colour pattern to be reconstructed from melanosomes.

taxa.name: Globigerinina
taxa.note: Planktic foraminifera colonise the open water column, becoming a permanent part of the ocean's carbon cycle.

first_appearances: Planktic foraminifera and coccolithophore-dominated open ocean
Salamanders and early frogs in numbers
extinctions: Modest turnover; no major extinction event in this interval

life.summary: The classic dinosaur world. The Morrison Formation holds Brachiosaurus, Apatosaurus, Diplodocus, Stegosaurus and Allosaurus in a seasonally dry conifer-and-fern landscape, and Tendaguru in Tanzania holds a strikingly similar fauna, showing how connected the continents still are. Solnhofen's lagoon preserves Archaeopteryx, pterosaurs and horseshoe crabs with their death trackways. Along the northern Tethys shelf a ten-thousand-kilometre belt of glass-sponge reefs forms the largest bioconstruction known. Pliosaurs like Liopleurodon are the sea's apex predators. Still no flowering plants and no grass.

taxa.name: Archaeopteryx lithographica
taxa.note: Feathers, wings and a long bony tail with teeth: the fossil that made evolution's prediction of transitional forms concrete.

taxa.name: Brachiosaurus
taxa.note: A sauropod holding its neck high above the canopy, weighing perhaps thirty tonnes.

taxa.name: Stegosaurus
taxa.note: Plated, spike-tailed, and with a brain famously small relative to its bulk.

taxa.name: Allosaurus
taxa.note: The dominant Morrison predator, known from dozens of individuals at the Cleveland-Lloyd quarry.

taxa.name: Liopleurodon
taxa.note: A short-necked pliosaur with a skull well over a metre long, hunting other marine reptiles.

taxa.name: Hexactinellida
taxa.note: Glass sponges building a reef belt along the Tethyan shelf larger than any reef system before or since.

taxa.name: Pterodactylus
taxa.note: A small short-tailed pterosaur from Solnhofen, and the first pterosaur ever described.

taxa.name: Docodonta
taxa.note: Small mammaliaforms with complex molars, exploiting insect and plant food in the dinosaurs' shadow.

extinctions: Jurassic-Cretaceous boundary turnover: moderate marine losses during a cool, low sea-level interval

life.summary: Flowering plants appear and begin their takeover, starting as small weedy colonisers of disturbed riverbanks rather than canopy trees. The Jehol Biota of northeastern China preserves the single most informative window on this world: feathered dinosaurs by the hundred, early birds, gliding mammals, and the first flowers, all entombed in volcanic ash and lake sediment. Rudist bivalves displace corals as the main tropical reef builder. Polar forests support dinosaurs living through months of winter darkness at high latitudes, because there is no ice at either pole. Gondwana is breaking up, and its dinosaur faunas start diverging from the northern ones.

taxa.name: Archaefructus
taxa.note: An aquatic Jehol plant that is among the earliest fossils confidently identified as a flowering plant.

taxa.name: Microraptor
taxa.note: A four-winged dromaeosaur with flight feathers on both fore and hind limbs, glossy black in life.

taxa.name: Repenomamus
taxa.note: A badger-sized Jehol mammal found with a juvenile dinosaur in its stomach -- Mesozoic mammals were not all prey.

taxa.name: Iguanodon
taxa.note: A large ornithopod with a thumb spike, and one of the first dinosaurs recognised as such.

taxa.name: Rudistes
taxa.note: Cone- and horn-shaped bivalves that crowd out corals and build the tropical reefs of the Cretaceous.

taxa.name: Confuciusornis
taxa.note: An early beaked bird known from thousands of specimens, many with long ornamental tail streamers.

taxa.name: Sinosauropteryx
taxa.note: The first dinosaur found with unambiguous filamentous feathers, and later with its ginger-and-white banded tail decoded.

taxa.name: Ornithocheiridae
taxa.note: Large fish-eating pterosaurs patrolling Cretaceous coastlines.

extinctions: Loss of many Jurassic sauropod and stegosaur lineages
Weissert and Selli oceanic anoxic events with marine turnover

life.summary: Angiosperms take the canopy and restructure terrestrial ecosystems around themselves, driving co-radiations of pollinating insects, and modern-looking bees, ants and butterflies appear. Dinosaurs reach their greatest diversity: tyrannosaurs, ceratopsians, hadrosaurs and titanosaurs, with mosasaurs taking over the seas as ichthyosaurs disappear. Sea level peaks and chalk accumulates over drowned continents. Then Chicxulub strikes the Yucatan while the Deccan Traps are erupting, and roughly seventy-five percent of species disappear -- all non-avian dinosaurs, all pterosaurs, all ammonites, all mosasaurs and plesiosaurs, and nearly all the calcareous plankton, which shuts down the ocean's carbon pump for hundreds of thousands of years.

taxa.name: Tyrannosaurus rex
taxa.note: Twelve metres, bone-crushing bite, binocular vision, and among the last non-avian dinosaurs to exist.

taxa.name: Triceratops
taxa.note: A horned, frilled ceratopsian and one of the most abundant large animals in the final Cretaceous ecosystems.

taxa.name: Mosasaurus
taxa.note: A giant marine lizard, related to monitors and snakes, that takes over the sea in the last twenty million years of the era.

taxa.name: Quetzalcoatlus
taxa.note: A pterosaur the size of a small aircraft, standing as tall as a giraffe and probably foraging on foot.

taxa.name: Ammonoidea
taxa.note: After 340 million years and countless species, ammonites end at the K-Pg boundary.

taxa.name: Vegavis iaai
taxa.note: An Antarctic fossil placing modern bird lineages -- specifically waterfowl relatives -- before the extinction.

taxa.name: Spinosaurus aegyptiacus
taxa.note: A sail-backed, paddle-tailed theropod that hunted fish in North African river systems.

taxa.name: Purgatorius
taxa.note: A small mammal at or near the base of the primate lineage, appearing right at the boundary.

extinctions: K-Pg mass extinction (~66 Ma): ~75% of species
All non-avian dinosaurs
All pterosaurs
Ammonites and belemnites
Mosasaurs and plesiosaurs
Rudists
Most calcareous nannoplankton and planktic foraminifera

life.summary: An empty world refilling. Ferns blanket the devastated landscape immediately after the impact, then forests return, and within a few million years mammals have gone from shrew-sized to bear-sized. The radiation is fast but strange: most Paleocene mammals belong to groups with no living descendants -- multituberculates, condylarths, taeniodonts. Birds also radiate, and in South America the flightless phorusrhacids start down the road to becoming apex predators. Cerrejón in Colombia preserves a tropical rainforest with Titanoboa, a thirteen-metre snake whose size implies mean annual temperatures well above anything today. The ocean's plankton slowly rebuilds.

taxa.name: Titanoboa cerrejonensis
taxa.note: A thirteen-metre, tonne-weight constrictor whose bulk is itself a thermometer for Paleocene tropical heat.

taxa.name: Multituberculata
taxa.note: Rodent-like mammals that had thrived alongside dinosaurs and now briefly dominate, before rodents outcompete them.

taxa.name: Condylarthra
taxa.note: A wastebasket of archaic hoofed mammals from which most modern ungulate groups eventually emerge.

taxa.name: Plesiadapiformes
taxa.note: Squirrel-like early primate relatives, arboreal and probably nocturnal.

taxa.name: Gastornis
taxa.note: A large flightless bird once assumed to be a predator, now thought to have been a heavy-billed herbivore.

taxa.name: Nummulites
taxa.note: Coin-sized benthic foraminifera beginning the bank-building that will define Tethyan shelf carbonates.

taxa.name: Carpolestes
taxa.note: A small primate relative with a grasping foot and a nail instead of a claw -- primate hands begin here.

extinctions: Continued attrition of Cretaceous holdover lineages
Benthic foraminiferal extinction at the very end (PETM onset)

life.summary: The warmest sustained interval of the Cenozoic. Palms grow in the Arctic, crocodilians live on Ellesmere Island, and paratropical rainforest reaches the mid-latitudes. Modern mammal orders appear essentially all at once at the Paleocene-Eocene boundary -- primates, artiodactyls, perissodactyls -- and Messel, Green River and the Willwood beds preserve them in exceptional detail. Whales complete the return to the sea within about ten million years, from the semi-aquatic Pakicetus to the fully marine Basilosaurus. Bats appear already capable of flight and echolocation. The interval ends in sharp cooling as Antarctic ice forms and the Grande Coupure turns over Eurasian faunas.

taxa.name: Basilosaurus
taxa.note: An eighteen-metre fully aquatic archaeocete with vestigial hind limbs, preserved by the hundred at Wadi Al-Hitan.

taxa.name: Darwinius masillae
taxa.note: An exquisitely complete Messel primate, gut contents and all, from near the base of the primate radiation.

taxa.name: Icaronycteris
taxa.note: An early bat from Green River with fully modern wings and evidence of echolocation.

taxa.name: Hyracotherium
taxa.note: The dog-sized ancestral horse, browsing in closed forest on four toes.

taxa.name: Azolla
taxa.note: A floating freshwater fern whose Arctic Ocean blooms buried enough carbon to help end the Eocene hothouse.

taxa.name: Uintatherium
taxa.note: A rhino-sized herbivore with six blunt horns and sabre-like canines, belonging to no surviving group.

taxa.name: Nothofagus
taxa.note: Southern beech forest growing on Antarctica at high southern latitudes -- forest on a continent now under ice.

taxa.name: Nummulites
taxa.note: Builds carbonate banks across the Tethys so thick the Egyptians later quarried them for the pyramids.

first_appearances: Modern primate, artiodactyl and perissodactyl orders
Grasses expanding, though not yet grassland
extinctions: Eocene-Oligocene transition (~34 Ma) extinction and cooling
Grande Coupure faunal turnover in Eurasia
Archaic Paleocene mammal groups largely eliminated

life.summary: The world cools and dries and opens up. The East Antarctic ice sheet becomes a permanent feature, closed forest retreats toward the tropics, and open woodland and the first grass-dominated habitats appear in continental interiors. Mammals respond with longer legs, higher-crowned teeth and larger bodies: the White River fauna of the North American badlands has Megacerops, Mesohippus and Archaeotherium. Paraceratherium, a hornless rhinoceros relative and the largest land mammal ever, browses in Asia. In South America, isolated since the Cretaceous, caviomorph rodents and platyrrhine monkeys arrive by rafting across the Atlantic and radiate on their own. Kelp forests develop in cool coastal upwelling zones.

taxa.name: Paraceratherium
taxa.note: A hornless rhinocerotoid five metres at the shoulder and around twenty tonnes -- the largest land mammal known.

taxa.name: Megacerops
taxa.note: A massive brontothere with a forked nasal horn, abundant in the White River badlands and extinct by the mid-Oligocene.

taxa.name: Mesohippus
taxa.note: A three-toed horse with teeth intermediate between browsing and grazing, tracking the opening landscape.

taxa.name: Aegyptopithecus
taxa.note: A Fayum catarrhine near the base of the Old World monkey and ape split.

taxa.name: Platyrrhini
taxa.note: New World monkeys, arriving in South America by transatlantic rafting and radiating in isolation.

taxa.name: Macrocystis
taxa.note: Giant kelp; kelp forests establish as a new nearshore biome in newly cool coastal waters.

taxa.name: Enaliarctos
taxa.note: An early pinniped, at the transition of carnivorans into fully marine life.

first_appearances: New World monkeys and caviomorph rodents in South America
extinctions: Brontotheres
Many archaic Eocene forest-adapted mammal lineages

life.summary: Grasslands take over the world. Open, grazed, fire-maintained landscapes spread on every continent, and between roughly eight and three million years ago C4 grasses expand globally -- a shift in photosynthetic chemistry visible directly in the carbon isotopes of fossil tooth enamel. Herbivores respond with ever-higher-crowned teeth, and horses go from browsers to grazers. Apes radiate widely across Africa and Eurasia, then contract, and the hominin lineage splits from chimpanzees near the end of the interval. The sea has Megalodon, and Australia's Riversleigh deposits preserve a rainforest fauna of marsupials that the continent's later drying would destroy.

taxa.name: Proconsul
taxa.note: An early African ape without a tail, near the base of the hominoid radiation.

taxa.name: Sahelanthropus tchadensis
taxa.note: A Chadian skull around seven million years old, close to the chimpanzee-human split and arguably on our side of it.

taxa.name: Otodus megalodon
taxa.note: A macropredatory shark perhaps sixteen metres long, known almost entirely from its teeth.

taxa.name: Poaceae (C4 lineages)
taxa.note: Grasses using C4 photosynthesis expand worldwide, remaking terrestrial ecosystems from the ground up.

taxa.name: Hipparion
taxa.note: A three-toed grazing horse whose rapid spread across the Old World is a datable event in its own right.

taxa.name: Deinotherium
taxa.note: A proboscidean with downward-curving lower tusks, unrelated to any surviving elephant lineage.

taxa.name: Obdurodon
taxa.note: A Riversleigh platypus that, unlike the living one, kept functional teeth as an adult.

taxa.name: Thalassocnus
taxa.note: A marine ground sloth that grazed seagrass off the Peruvian coast -- a lineage no one predicted.

first_appearances: Hypsodont grazing dentition across many lineages
extinctions: Middle Miocene disruption and cooling
Contraction of Eurasian ape diversity
Loss of much Australian rainforest fauna as the continent dries

life.summary: The world assembles into something recognisable. The Isthmus of Panama closes, rerouting ocean currents and launching the Great American Biotic Interchange -- North American carnivorans pour south, and ground sloths, glyptodonts and armadillos move north. Northern Hemisphere glaciation begins around 2.7 million years ago and the boreal forest and tundra biomes come into existence. In Africa, Australopithecus walks upright across savanna at Laetoli, leaving footprints in volcanic ash that show a modern striding gait. The first stone tools appear near the end of the interval, and with them the genus Homo.

taxa.name: Australopithecus afarensis
taxa.note: Lucy's species: bipedal, small-brained, and the maker of the Laetoli footprint trail.

taxa.name: Megatherium
taxa.note: A ground sloth the size of an elephant, rearing up to pull down branches.

taxa.name: Smilodon
taxa.note: The sabre-toothed cat, moving south into a South America that had never seen anything like it.

taxa.name: Titanis walleri
taxa.note: A terror bird moving north across the new isthmus -- the interchange ran both ways.

taxa.name: Glyptodon
taxa.note: An armoured, car-sized relative of armadillos, spreading north with the interchange.

taxa.name: Homo habilis
taxa.note: Associated with the earliest widely accepted stone tool industries, right at the interval's close.

taxa.name: Mammuthus
taxa.note: Mammoths spread across the newly cold northern continents as the mammoth steppe forms.

extinctions: Pliocene marine megafauna extinction, including Megalodon
Loss of much warm-adapted northern flora as cooling sets in

life.summary: Ice sheets advance and retreat on orbital cycles, repeatedly rearranging every terrestrial biome. The mammoth steppe -- a cold, dry, productive grassland with no modern analogue -- stretches from Iberia to Alaska, supporting mammoth, woolly rhinoceros, steppe bison and horse. Hominins spread out of Africa repeatedly; Homo sapiens appears by around 315,000 years ago and reaches every continent except Antarctica. Then, in a pattern that tracks human arrival more closely than it tracks climate, the large-bodied fauna disappears: Australia's around 46,000 years ago, the Americas' around 13,000, with Africa least affected because its animals evolved alongside hominins. The current extinction pulse continues, now driven by habitat loss and climate change.

taxa.name: Homo sapiens
taxa.note: The only species to have become a global biome in its own right, and the proximate cause of the extinction it is documenting.

taxa.name: Homo neanderthalensis
taxa.note: Cold-adapted Eurasian hominins who buried their dead, made pigment and left DNA in most living non-African people.

taxa.name: Mammuthus primigenius
taxa.note: The woolly mammoth, keystone grazer of the mammoth steppe, surviving on Wrangel Island until about 4,000 years ago.

taxa.name: Diprotodon
taxa.note: A three-tonne wombat relative, the largest marsupial ever, gone from Australia around 46,000 years ago.

taxa.name: Smilodon fatalis
taxa.note: The Rancho La Brea sabre-tooth, known from thousands of individuals trapped in asphalt seeps.

taxa.name: Varanus priscus
taxa.note: A seven-metre monitor lizard, Australia's largest terrestrial predator until the megafauna extinction.

taxa.name: Genyornis newtoni
taxa.note: A flightless Australian bird whose burnt eggshell is among the more direct evidence linking humans to the extinctions.

taxa.name: Coelodonta antiquitatis
taxa.note: The woolly rhinoceros, its appearance known from cave paintings as well as bones.

extinctions: Late Quaternary megafauna extinction on every continent except Africa
Neanderthals and Denisovans
Ongoing anthropogenic extinction pulse

Laurentia.text: The Cambrian record here is exceptional. Archaeocyath reefs fringe the tropical shelf, olenellid trilobites define the faunal province, and at roughly 508 Ma the Burgess Shale of British Columbia captures an entire soft-bodied community -- Anomalocaris, Opabinia, Hallucigenia, Wiwaxia -- in a mudslide at the foot of a carbonate escarpment. Sirius Passet in North Greenland preserves an older, equally remarkable assemblage.

The Sauk Sea floods the craton, laying down sheets of clean quartz sand and then carbonate across a drowned, lifeless continent. The Ibex section in Utah and the St. George Group of Newfoundland record the opening stages of the Ordovician radiation in conodonts, brachiopods and nautiloids.

Carbonate platforms across the craton fill with bryozoans, crinoids and articulate brachiopods as diversification peaks. Giant straight-shelled nautiloids hunt the shelf. The Taconic arc collides along the eastern margin and starts shedding clastics westward.

The Cincinnatian series of Ohio, Indiana and Kentucky is one of the best-sampled shallow marine faunas in the world -- dense brachiopod, bryozoan and crinoid assemblages. Beecher's Trilobite Bed in New York preserves trilobite appendages in pyrite. At the top, the Hirnantian glaciation drains the epeiric sea and the fauna collapses.

Silurian reefs rebuild: the Michigan Basin pinnacle reefs and the Rochester Shale of New York. The Bertie Group lagoons of New York and Ontario preserve Eurypterus remipes in extraordinary numbers, the state fossil of New York and the type setting for sea scorpions.

Ediacaran and latest Precambrian strata of the Mackenzie and Wernecke Mountains carry rare frondose fossils, cap carbonates over Cryogenian tillites, and the trace fossils that mark the first burrowing. The record is real but sparse compared with Avalonia or the White Sea.

Baltica.text: The Alum Shale of Sweden is a black, organic-rich, slowly deposited unit packed with olenid trilobites adapted to low oxygen. Within it the Orsten fauna preserves millimetre-scale crustaceans and larvae in three dimensions in phosphate -- limbs, setae and all -- the finest preservation of Cambrian microarthropods anywhere.

The orthoceratite limestones of Sweden and Estonia are condensed, cool-water carbonates crowded with straight-shelled nautiloids, and are the classic Baltoscandian Ordovician section. The Thorsberg quarry in Sweden yields fossil meteorites from a mid-Ordovician asteroid breakup, embedded in the same beds.
Estonian and Swedish carbonate platforms hold rich bryozoan, brachiopod and echinoderm faunas, then record the Hirnantia fauna and the end-Ordovician extinction in continuous section.

Gotland is the outstanding Silurian reef exposure on Earth: stromatoporoid and tabulate coral bioherms with intact fore-reef and lagoon facies, plus abundant eurypterids, nautiloids and early vascular plant debris.

The White Sea coast of northern Russia yields the richest Ediacaran assemblage known -- Dickinsonia, Kimberella, Charnia and Yorgia preserved on sandstone soles, together with grazing traces showing Kimberella actively scraping microbial mats. This is the strongest evidence that some Ediacaran organisms were animals that moved.

Siberia.text: The Siberian Platform holds the global reference sections for the earliest Cambrian: the Tommotian small shelly fossil assemblages and enormous archaeocyath reef complexes along the Aldan and Lena rivers. Much of the standard early Cambrian timescale was built here.

The Sinsk Biota, a Botoman-age lagerstatte, preserves a soft-bodied community drowned by an anoxic event on the platform margin -- sponges, algae, arthropods and eldonioids, older than the Burgess Shale.

Ordovician carbonates carry endemic brachiopod, ostracod and trilobite faunas distinct from Laurentia's and Baltica's, reflecting Siberia's isolation as an independent continent through most of the Palaeozoic.
Silurian reef and shelf faunas continue in warm low-latitude carbonates, still with a strongly endemic character.

Avalonia.text: Mistaken Point in Newfoundland is the defining Ediacaran deep-water site: rangeomorph fronds preserved in life position under ash falls, at 574 to 560 Ma the oldest large complex organisms known anywhere. Charnwood Forest in England yields Charnia masoni, the fossil that in 1957 proved Precambrian rocks contain complex life.

Ordovician graptolite shales of Wales and southern Britain are the type sections for the entire graptolite biostratigraphic scheme, alongside distinctive cold-water trilobite and brachiopod faunas reflecting Avalonia's high-latitude Gondwanan origin.
As Avalonia rafts north across the Rheic Ocean its faunas warm and progressively merge with Baltica's -- the fossil record itself tracks the plate motion.

The Ludlow Bone Bed of Shropshire is a thin, spectacular concentration of early vertebrate scales and spines. Nearby, the Welsh Borderland yields Cooksonia, among the earliest vascular land plants, in the same rocks.

Gondwana.text: The Emu Bay Shale of South Australia preserves soft-bodied Cambrian animals including Anomalocaris specimens with their compound eyes intact -- tens of thousands of lenses each, showing these were highly visual predators. Archaeocyath reefs fringe the Australian and Antarctic margins.

The Fezouata Biota of Morocco, at around 478 Ma, extends Burgess-type soft-bodied preservation into the Ordovician and shows the same body plans persisting alongside the new Palaeozoic fauna. Cold-water shelf faunas cover North Africa, and at the end of the interval the Hirnantian ice cap sits over the Sahara, leaving glacial pavements still visible in Algeria and Libya.

The Malvinokaffric Realm -- a distinct cold-water province across South America, South Africa and the Falklands -- develops low-diversity brachiopod and trilobite faunas quite unlike the tropical assemblages of Laurentia. Baragwanathia, a surprisingly advanced lycophyte, appears in Victoria, Australia.

The Bokkeveld Group of South Africa and the Parana Basin of Brazil hold classic Malvinokaffric Devonian faunas. In Western Australia the Gogo Formation preserves Devonian fish in uncrushed three dimensions inside limestone nodules, including Materpiscis with an embryo and mineralised umbilical cord -- the oldest known vertebrate pregnancy.

The Dwyka tillites of southern Africa and their equivalents in South America, India, Australia and Antarctica record the Late Palaeozoic Ice Age; their matching glacial striations across now-separate continents were core evidence for Gondwana. Post-glacial floras begin with Botrychiopsis and Gangamopteris.

The definitive Gondwanan interval: Glossopteris forest across all five fragments, and Mesosaurus, a small freshwater reptile, in the Whitehill Formation of South Africa and the Irati Formation of Brazil -- an animal that could not have crossed an ocean, found on both sides of the modern Atlantic. The Karoo Basin records therapsid faunas in near-continuous succession up to the extinction.

The Karoo's Lystrosaurus Assemblage Zone documents the end-Permian recovery on land better than anywhere else. The Dicroidium flora spreads across Gondwana, and Antarctic and Australian sections carry equivalent Triassic assemblages.

Gondwanan dinosaur faunas diverge from northern ones as the fragments separate. Tendaguru in Tanzania yields a Late Jurassic fauna strikingly similar to the Morrison's -- Giraffatitan, Dicraeosaurus, Kentrosaurus -- and Vulcanodon in Zimbabwe is among the earliest true sauropods.

Laurussia.text: The Old Red Sandstone continent: red alluvial plains with armoured jawless fish such as Cephalaspis and Pteraspis in the channels, and placoderms and acanthodians in the lakes. At around 407 Ma the Rhynie chert in Aberdeenshire silicifies an entire hot-spring wetland in growth position -- Rhynia, Aglaophyton, mites, springtails, a trigonotarbid and the oldest accepted insect, all preserved cell by cell.

Gilboa in New York preserves the stumps of the world's first forest, Wattieza-type cladoxylopsids rooted where they grew. The Hamilton Group of New York is one of the most intensively studied shallow marine faunas anywhere, with brachiopods, trilobites and corals through a long continuous section.

The interval that put vertebrates on land. Tiktaalik roseae comes from Ellesmere Island at about 375 Ma, found by predicting the right rock age and environment and going to look. Miguasha in Quebec yields Eusthenopteron and Elpistostege; East Greenland yields Acanthostega and Ichthyostega. The Frasnian-Famennian crisis destroys the reef systems recorded in the same basins.

East Kirkton in Scotland, a hot-spring lake deposit, yields Westlothiana and other early tetrapods from within Romer's Gap. Mississippian crinoidal limestones blanket the platform, and the Bear Gulch Limestone of Montana preserves an entire shallow marine fish community including bizarre chondrichthyans.

Pangaea.text: The coal age at its height. Joggins in Nova Scotia preserves upright lycopsid stumps with Hylonomus, the earliest amniote, fossilised inside the hollow trunks. Mazon Creek in Illinois yields soft-bodied animals in ironstone nodules, including the unclassifiable Tully monster. Meganeura and Arthropleura crawl and fly through swamps that oxygen levels above thirty percent make possible.

The Texas red beds -- Dimetrodon, Edaphosaurus, Eryops, Seymouria, Diplocaulus -- are the reference fauna for early synapsid-dominated terrestrial ecosystems. Bromacker in Germany yields an equivalent, exquisitely preserved upland fauna. In the sea, the Capitan reef complex of west Texas builds a bryozoan-sponge-algal barrier now exposed in the Guadalupe Mountains.

Therapsids take over. The Karoo's Tapinocephalus Assemblage Zone holds massive dinocephalians alongside early dicynodonts and the first gorgonopsians. Fusulinid foraminifera reach maximum size and diversity on the shelves, then are culled at the end-Guadalupian as the Emeishan Traps erupt.

The last Permian ecosystems: Dicynodon and Inostrancevia in the Karoo and the Russian platform, Glossopteris forest across the south, and the Zechstein Sea evaporating to salt in the arid interior. Then the Siberian Traps erupt and the Meishan section in South China records the extinction bed itself, dated to 251.9 Ma.

The extinction interval. Coal ceases to form anywhere on Earth, marine microbialites replace reefs, and the terrestrial record is dominated globally by Lystrosaurus. No other horizon in the Phanerozoic is so uniform across so many continents, and the uniformity is the point -- almost nothing else survived.

Laurasia.text: The Chinle Formation of the American Southwest preserves the Late Triassic in full: petrified Araucarioxylon logs, phytosaurs, aetosaurs, and Coelophysis by the hundred at Ghost Ranch. The Newark Supergroup rift lakes record cyclical wet and dry phases and dense dinosaur and pseudosuchian trackways along their margins.

The Blue Lias at Lyme Regis, worked by Mary Anning from the 1810s, produced the first recognised ichthyosaurs, plesiosaurs and British pterosaurs. Holzmaden's Posidonia Shale in Germany, laid down under the Toarcian anoxic event, preserves ichthyosaurs with soft-tissue outlines and females fossilised mid-birth.

The Morrison Formation of the western interior yields the canonical Late Jurassic dinosaur fauna -- Diplodocus, Apatosaurus, Brachiosaurus, Stegosaurus, Allosaurus -- from a seasonally dry conifer floodplain. Solnhofen in Bavaria, a hypersaline lagoon, preserves Archaeopteryx along with pterosaurs and horseshoe crabs still attached to their final trackways. The Oxford Clay of England holds pliosaurs and marine crocodiles.

North America.text: Hell Creek and Lance in Montana, the Dakotas and Wyoming record the final two million years of the Cretaceous with Tyrannosaurus rex, Triceratops, Edmontosaurus and Ankylosaurus, and then the iridium-bearing boundary clay directly above them. The Two Medicine Formation preserves Maiasaura nesting colonies with eggs, embryos and juveniles, the first solid evidence of dinosaur parental care.

The Fort Union Formation records the recovery: a fern spike, then rapid mammal diversification through the Puercan and Torrejonian faunas as body sizes climb from shrew to sheep within a few million years.

The Green River Formation's lake beds in Wyoming, Colorado and Utah yield fish, insects, birds, bats and plants in millions of laminated specimens. The Willwood Formation of the Bighorn Basin captures the PETM in continuous section, with dwarfed mammals through the warm interval and the first appearance of horses, primates and artiodactyls in North America.

The White River Group of the Badlands is the classic Oligocene mammal sequence: Megacerops, Mesohippus, Archaeotherium, Hyaenodon and oreodonts in aeolian and floodplain sediments, recording the shift to open, drier country.

Great Plains sequences track grassland expansion through mammal teeth, with horses moving from browsing to grazing dentition. Ashfall Fossil Beds in Nebraska, at about 12 Ma, preserves an entire waterhole community -- rhinos, horses, camels -- killed by ash from a Yellowstone-track eruption a thousand kilometres away and buried where they fell.
The Hagerman Horse Quarry in Idaho yields hundreds of Pliocene horses. Ground sloths, glyptodonts and armadillos arrive from South America as the Isthmus of Panama closes.

Rancho La Brea in Los Angeles has produced millions of specimens from asphalt seeps -- Smilodon, dire wolves, mammoths, Teratornis -- with predators outnumbering prey because each trapped herbivore drew in more carnivores. Mammoths, mastodons, giant ground sloths and horses disappear from the continent around 13,000 to 11,000 years ago, closely following human arrival.

South America.text: Patagonia yields the largest dinosaurs known: Argentinosaurus and Patagotitan among titanosaurs, and Giganotosaurus among predators, in a fauna dominated by abelisaurids rather than the tyrannosaurs of the north -- a direct consequence of Gondwanan isolation. The Crato and Santana Formations of Brazil preserve pterosaurs, fish and insects in limestone concretions with soft tissue intact.

Cerrejon in Colombia, at around 58 Ma, preserves the oldest known Neotropical rainforest, with Titanoboa cerrejonensis, a thirteen-metre snake whose body size implies a mean annual temperature well above any modern tropical forest. Tiupampa in Bolivia yields early South American mammals.

South America is an island continent, and its mammals evolve alone: notoungulates, litopterns and astrapotheres fill niches occupied elsewhere by hoofed mammals, with marsupial sparassodonts as the predators. Laguna del Hunco in Patagonia preserves a Gondwanan flora with clear Australian and Antarctic affinities.

The Deseadan fauna records the arrival of caviomorph rodents and platyrrhine monkeys, which reached the continent by rafting across the Atlantic and then radiated in isolation into everything from marmosets to capybaras.

The Santa Cruz Formation of Patagonia and La Venta in Colombia preserve rich Miocene faunas. The Pebas system, a vast wetland covering much of western Amazonia, holds Purussaurus, a caiman perhaps ten metres long, alongside giant turtles. Phorusrhacid terror birds remain apex predators.
The Great American Biotic Interchange runs in earnest: cats, bears, canids and camelids arrive from the north, and many endemic South American groups decline as a result.

Megatherium, Toxodon, Macrauchenia and Glyptodon dominate the Pleistocene, and Darwin's collection of these at Punta Alta during the Beagle voyage directly shaped his thinking about extinction and descent. Monte Verde in Chile carries securely dated human occupation by about 14,500 years ago, and the megafauna is gone shortly after.

Africa.text: The Kem Kem beds of Morocco, at roughly 100 Ma, hold an implausible concentration of large predators -- Spinosaurus, Carcharodontosaurus, Deltadromeus -- in a river and delta system rich enough in fish to support them. Bahariya in Egypt yields an equivalent fauna, most of it destroyed in a Munich museum in 1944 and only recently recollected.

Late Cretaceous continental faunas are patchily exposed, with titanosaurs and abelisaurids in Morocco, Egypt and Madagascar. Madagascar, isolated since about 88 Ma, develops its own strange fauna including Majungasaurus and Beelzebufo, a frog the size of a beach ball.

Wadi Al-Hitan in Egypt, the Valley of the Whales, preserves hundreds of archaeocetes including Basilosaurus with vestigial hind limbs -- the clearest fossil documentation of any major evolutionary transition. The Fayum Depression yields Aegyptopithecus and other early anthropoids, near the base of the monkey and ape radiation.

Rusinga Island in Kenya yields Proconsul, an early tailless ape, in Miocene forest. Late in the interval, Sahelanthropus tchadensis from Chad at around 7 Ma and Orrorin from Kenya sit close to the chimpanzee-human divergence, and the savanna biome that hominins evolve within assembles at the same time.

The richest hominin record anywhere. Laetoli in Tanzania preserves a 3.66 Ma trail of bipedal footprints in volcanic ash with a fully modern striding gait. Hadar in Ethiopia yields Lucy, and the Turkana Basin provides a near-continuous sequence of Australopithecus and early Homo alongside its fauna.

Olduvai Gorge and Koobi Fora record Homo habilis, Homo erectus and the Oldowan and Acheulean tool industries. Jebel Irhoud in Morocco pushes Homo sapiens back to about 315,000 years ago. Africa alone retains most of its large mammal fauna through the late Quaternary, most plausibly because its animals evolved alongside hominins and were never naive to them.

Eurasia.text: Messel in Germany, at about 47 Ma, preserves an entire Eocene lake ecosystem down to gut contents, fur, feathers and structural colour in beetles -- Darwinius, early horses, bats, and a pregnant mare with a foetus. The London Clay yields a tropical fruit and seed flora from what is now the Thames estuary.

The Grande Coupure at about 34 Ma turns over the European mammal fauna almost completely as cooling and falling sea level open land connections from Asia, replacing endemic Eocene lineages with immigrants.

Apes radiate widely -- Dryopithecus in Europe, Sivapithecus in Asia -- and then contract as forests give way to open country. The Pikermi and Samos faunas of Greece and Turkey are dominated by Hipparion, giraffids and hyaenids in an assemblage much like a modern African savanna, and the Messinian salinity crisis desiccates the Mediterranean at the interval's end.
Faunas modernise as cooling intensifies; the steppe and taiga biomes take shape across the northern interior.

The mammoth steppe stretches from Iberia to Beringia with mammoth, woolly rhinoceros, steppe bison and cave lion. Neanderthals occupy Europe and western Asia, Denisovans are identified from a finger bone and DNA at Denisova Cave in Siberia, and Chauvet and Lascaux record the animals of this world painted by people who lived among them.

Australia.text: Tingamarra in Queensland, at about 55 Ma, is the only substantial early Cenozoic mammal site on the continent and hints at a fauna with South American connections. After it the record goes nearly silent until the Oligocene, which is why the origins of Australia's marsupial groups are so poorly constrained.

Riversleigh in Queensland is a World Heritage sequence of cave and pool limestones preserving a Miocene rainforest fauna: Nimbadon, Obdurodon (a toothed platypus), early thylacinids, marsupial lions and enormous diversity of bats and possums. It documents a wet, forested Australia that the continent's later drying destroyed.
Aridification accelerates. The Chinchilla Sand fauna records the shift from rainforest to open woodland and grassland assemblages as the interior dries.

The Pleistocene megafauna: Diprotodon, a three-tonne wombat relative and the largest marsupial ever; Thylacoleo, the marsupial lion; Varanus priscus, a seven-metre monitor; Procoptodon, a short-faced kangaroo; and Genyornis, a flightless bird. Naracoorte Caves in South Australia preserve the assemblage in pitfall traps. Nearly all of it disappears around 46,000 to 40,000 years ago, shortly after human arrival and without a matching climate signal -- the clearest megafaunal extinction case anywhere.

Antarctica.text: The Hanson Formation in the Transantarctic Mountains yields Cryolophosaurus ellioti, a crested Early Jurassic theropod, along with sauropodomorphs and a tritylodont -- a full terrestrial vertebrate fauna at high southern latitude, on a continent with no ice.

The James Ross Basin off the Antarctic Peninsula preserves a Late Cretaceous marine and coastal fauna with mosasaurs, plesiosaurs, ammonites and the armoured dinosaur Antarctopelta. Vegavis iaai from Vega Island at about 68 Ma is a waterfowl relative, and the strongest evidence that modern bird lineages existed before the K-Pg extinction.

The La Meseta Formation on Seymour Island is the key Eocene site on the continent: Nothofagus southern beech forest, large penguins including Palaeeudyptes, marsupials such as Antarctodolops, and a diverse marine invertebrate fauna. Antarctica at this point is forested, temperate and connected to South America.
The ice sheet establishes. Nothofagus persists in tundra-like form for a time and then vanishes, and the terrestrial fossil record of the continent effectively ends.

Nothing terrestrial except contested Nothofagus wood and diatoms in the Sirius Group, argued over as evidence for a warmer Pliocene interval. The marine record from surrounding basins continues, but the continent itself becomes a fossil blank.

India.text: The Lameta Formation, interbedded with the Deccan lavas, preserves titanosaur nesting grounds with thousands of eggs, plus the snake Sanajeh coiled around a hatching sauropod egg -- direct evidence of predation on dinosaur nests. India at this point is an island continent drifting north.

The Cambay Shale lignites at Vastan in Gujarat, around 54 Ma, preserve amber with insects, early primates, bats and the earliest artiodactyls, on an India that has just docked or is about to. The fauna shows unexpected connections to Europe and Asia rather than deep isolation.

The Siwalik Group along the Himalayan front is one of the longest continuous terrestrial mammal sequences on Earth. It records Sivapithecus (close to the orangutan lineage), Sivatherium, the Hipparion immigration datum, and the shift from C3 browsing to C4 grazing diets written directly in tooth enamel isotopes.

Upper Siwalik faunas continue into the Pleistocene with Stegodon, Elephas and large bovids. The Narmada Valley yields a hominin calvaria, one of the few substantial Middle Pleistocene human fossils from the subcontinent.

Cimmeria.text: A ribbon of terranes still attached to Gondwana's northern margin, carrying cool-water Permian faunas and Glossopteris flora -- their fossils are how the terranes are identified as Gondwanan at all, despite now sitting in Turkey, Iran and Tibet.

As the ribbon rifts away and drifts north, its faunas shift from Gondwanan cold-water to Tethyan warm-water, and Triassic carbonate platforms with scleractinian reefs develop along its margins. The fossil record here tracks a continent changing latitude.

North China.text: Cambrian shelf carbonates of Shandong and Hebei, including the Zhangxia and Gushan formations, hold classic trilobite faunas that underpin the East Asian Cambrian biostratigraphic scheme.
The Majiagou carbonates record a broad Ordovician epeiric platform, followed by a long depositional hiatus that removes most of the mid-Palaeozoic record from the craton.

Carboniferous and Permian coal measures of Shanxi carry the Cathaysian flora, including Gigantopteris with its broad net-veined leaves -- an isolated wet-tropical flora surviving while the rest of Pangaea dried out.
Triassic red beds yield Sinokannemeyeria and other dicynodonts, plus early archosaurs, recording the post-extinction recovery on the northern Chinese blocks.

The Jehol Biota of western Liaoning is arguably the most important fossil deposit of the last century. Volcanic ash and lake sediment preserve feathered dinosaurs (Sinosauropteryx, Microraptor), early birds (Confuciusornis), mammals that ate dinosaurs (Repenomamus), pterosaurs, and the early flowering plant Archaefructus -- with feathers, fur and even melanosomes intact.

South China.text: The Doushantuo Formation phosphorites preserve the Weng'an biota: multicellular algae, acritarchs and controversial embryo-like fossils, some interpreted as animal embryos and others as giant sulphur bacteria. Whatever they are, they are cellular-level preservation from 600 million years ago.

The Lantian and Miaohe biotas preserve macroscopic algae and possible early animals, and the Dengying Formation of the Yangtze Gorges carries late Ediacaran skeletal fossils and the Ediacaran-Cambrian boundary in continuous marine section.

Chengjiang in Yunnan, at about 518 Ma, is the earliest of the great Cambrian lagerstatten -- Anomalocaris, Hallucigenia, and critically Myllokunmingia and Haikouichthys, the oldest known vertebrates. Xiaoshiba nearby adds more. Together with the Burgess Shale these deposits are most of what is known about the Cambrian explosion's soft-bodied cast.
The Kaili Biota of Guizhou, at around 508 Ma, bridges the gap between Chengjiang and the Burgess Shale in both age and faunal composition.

The Meishan section in Zhejiang is the global stratotype for the Permian-Triassic boundary, recording the end-Permian extinction bed with a precision no other section matches. The Emeishan Traps erupt through the block at the end-Guadalupian.

Triassic marine reptile faunas are exceptional here: the Luoping Biota at about 244 Ma and the Guanling Biota at about 235 Ma preserve ichthyosaurs, thalattosaurs, Keichousaurus and complete crinoid colonies, documenting the recovery of marine ecosystems after the extinction in unusual detail.

Amazonia.text: The Amazonian craton is a stable, largely emergent block through the Neoproterozoic, and its fossil record is correspondingly thin -- stromatolites and microbial carbonates in marginal basins, and Cryogenian glacial deposits with cap carbonates in the surrounding Paraguay and Araguaia belts. There is essentially no body fossil record from the craton interior; this is a region defined by what it lacks.

Congo Craton.text: The Otavi Group along the craton's southern margin in Namibia is a reference section for Snowball Earth: the Chuos and Ghaub diamictites capped by carbonates deposited in the super-greenhouse aftermath, with microbial and stromatolitic communities recording the recovery. Fossils are microbial rather than metazoan.

The Mbuji-Mayi Supergroup in the Democratic Republic of the Congo yields Tonian acritarchs, vase-shaped microfossils and stromatolites -- a modest but genuine window on Neoproterozoic eukaryotes from the African interior. Coverage is poor and much of the craton's Precambrian record remains unstudied.

Kalahari Craton.text: The Nama Group of Namibia is one of the most important Ediacaran successions anywhere. It holds Cloudina and Namacalathus -- the first calcareous skeletons and the first animal-built reefs -- along with Pteridinium, Rangea and Swartpuntia, and drill holes in Cloudina tubes that are the oldest direct evidence of predation on a skeletonised animal. The section runs continuously into the Cambrian.

The Port Nolloth and Numees successions record Cryogenian glaciation on the craton margin, with diamictites and cap carbonates. Earlier Neoproterozoic strata are sparsely fossiliferous, holding stromatolites and microbial laminites rather than anything larger.

Baltica.shared: Paradoxides marks the cold-water province Baltica shared with Avalonia and Gondwana, distinct from Laurentia's Olenellus fauna - the split that revealed the Iapetus Ocean.

Siberian archaeocyath reefs are the largest and best-dated of the Early Cambrian world.

Avalonia.shared: Avalonia's cold-water fauna groups it with Gondwana and Baltica, across the Iapetus from Laurentia.
